Higher-Order Godbersen Inequality and a characterization of simplices via the face lattice

Filip Fryš Address: Mathematical Institute, Faculty of Mathematics and Physics, Charles University, Prague, Czechia Email address: filip.frys@matfyz.cuni.cz , Jan Kotrbatý Address: Mathematical Institute, Faculty of Mathematics and Physics, Charles University, Prague, Czechia Email address: kotrbaty@karlin.mff.cuni.cz , Mohamed A. Mouamine Address: Mathematical Institute, Faculty of Mathematics and Physics, Charles University, Prague, Czechia Email address: mohamed-abdeldjalil.mouamine@matfyz.cuni.cz and Shouda Wang Address: Department of Mathematics, KTH Royal Institute of Technology Email address: shoudawang@princeton.edu
Abstract.

We settle the long-standing Godbersen conjecture that the mixed volume of a convex body of fixed positive volume with its reflection about the origin is maximized precisely by simplices. For the proof, we establish a new characterization of simplices by a natural incidence relation on the face lattice. Moreover, we establish a higher-order generalization of the Godbersen inequality and show that simplices are the only nontrivial equality cases, confirming a conjecture of Schneider from 2000.

1. Introduction

Simplices are among the most fundamental objects in convex geometry and their characterization has been a central theme of study in the field. One important approach of characterization is to define the simplex as the unique extremizer of a geometric inequality. A first example is the Minkowski asymmetry measure of a full-dimensional convex body K⊆ℝnK\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} given by

s⁡(K):=inf{t>0:−K⊆t​K+x​ for some ​x∈ℝn},s(K):=\inf\{t>0:-K\subseteq tK+x\text{ for some }x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\},

where −K-K is the reflection of KK about the origin. It satisfies s⁡(K)≤ns(K)\leq n and equality holds if and only if KK is a simplex, see [13, §6.1]. Further inequalities having simplices as their minimizers include Ball’s reverse isoperimetric inequality [4], Grünbaum’s inequality [13], Zhang’s projection inequality [34], the Mahler inequality [19], and many more.

Our present work is motivated by yet another such inequality. For a convex body K⊆ℝnK\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} we write Vn⁡(K)\operatorname{V}_{n}(K) for its volume and define the difference body K−K:={x−y:x,y∈K}K-K:=\{x-y:x,y\in K\}. The celebrated Rogers–Shephard inequality [21, 22] bounds the volume of the difference body by the volume of KK itself:

(1) Vn⁡(K−K)≤(2​nn)​Vn⁡(K).\operatorname{V}_{n}(K-K)\leq\binom{2n}{n}\operatorname{V}_{n}(K).

If KK is full-dimensional, then equality holds in (1) if and only if KK is a simplex. Let us also mention that the Brunn–Minkowski inequality gives a sharp lower bound on Vn⁡(K−K)\operatorname{V}_{n}(K-K), namely Vn⁡(K−K)≥2n​Vn⁡(K)\operatorname{V}_{n}(K-K)\geq 2^{n}\operatorname{V}_{n}(K), with equality if and only if KK is centrally symmetric or lower-dimensional.

A conjecture of Godbersen [12], which predates the proof of the Rogers–Shephard inequality, speculated a refinement of (1). Let Vn\operatorname{V}_{n} denote the mixed volume, i.e., the Minkowski-multilinear, symmetric polarization of the volume. Since K−K=K+(−K)K-K=K+(-K), the multilinearity of mixed volume yields Vn⁡(K−K)=∑k=0n(nk)​Vn​(K⁡[k],−K⁡[n−k])\operatorname{V}_{n}(K-K)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}\operatorname{V}_{n}(K[k],\allowbreak-K[n-k]), where K⁡[k]K[k] denotes kk repetitions of KK. On the other hand, (2​nn)=∑k=0n(nk)2\binom{2n}{n}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}^{2}. Comparing the two sums, Godbersen [12] in 1938, and independently Makai Jr. [14] in 1974, conjectured that (1) in fact holds term-wise; see (2) below.

A priori, this stronger family of inequalities may have many more extremizers than (1). In addition, it is often the case that inequalities involving mixed volumes have a large number of intricate equality cases that are not straightforward to describe, cf. [28, 29, 31, 8, 30, 18, 32]. Nevertheless, it was commonly conjectured that the only nontrivial equality cases should still be simplices, see, e.g., [7, §23.1.3] and [27, §10.1]. The following inequality together with equality characterization is thus commonly referred to as the Godbersen conjecture.

Conjecture 1.1 (Godbersen conjecture).

Let 0≤k≤n0\leq k\leq n. For any convex body K⊆ℝnK\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}, one has

(2) Vn⁡(K⁡[k],−K⁡[n−k])≤(nk)​Vn⁡(K).\operatorname{V}_{n}\bigl(K[k],-K[n-k]\bigr)\leq\binom{n}{k}\operatorname{V}_{n}(K).

If 1≤k≤n−11\leq k\leq n-1 and KK is full-dimensional, then equality holds if and only if KK is a simplex.

Note that if KK is lower-dimensional, then both sides of (2) are equal to zero. If k∈{0,n}k\in\{0,n\} then the mixed volume on the left-hand side of (2) is just the volume of KK and hence equality holds for any KK. Moreover, the cases k∈{1,n−1}k\in\{1,n-1\} follow at once from the inequality s⁡(K)≤ns(K)\leq n for the Minkowski asymmetry measure.

Despite its long history, most of the progress on the Godbersen conjecture has only been made rather recently. This includes a weaker general bound on the left-hand side of (2) due to Artstein-Avidan, Einhorn, Florentin, and Ostrover [1], a proof for anti-blocking and locally anti-blocking convex bodies by Artstein-Avidan, Sadovsky, and Sanyal [3, 23], and averaged forms of the conjecture due to Artstein-Avidan and Putterman [2]. Very recently, the second- and third-named authors [17] proved the inequality (2) for all convex bodies and characterized equality among polytopes.

In the present paper, we completely characterize the equality cases of (2) for general convex bodies and thus settle the Godbersen conjecture in full generality. Furthermore, we prove a more general version of Conjecture 1.1, where KK and −K-K are replaced by an array of natural embeddings of KK into a product space, which was conjectured by Schneider [26] in 2000. A particularly interesting by-product of the proof is a new characterization of the simplex via the structure of its face lattice.

1.1. Equality cases of the Godbersen inequality

Our first main result resolves the equality cases part of Conjecture 1.1.

Theorem 1.2.

Let K⊆ℝnK\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} be a full-dimensional convex body and let 1≤k≤n−11\leq k\leq n-1. Equality in (2) holds if and only if KK is a simplex.

In order to outline the strategy of our proof of Theorem 1.2, let us briefly recall the proof of (2) given in [17]. The proof repeatedly uses the following monotonicity property for mixed volumes: for convex bodies L,M,C1,…,Cn−1⊆ℝnL,M,C_{1},\dots,C_{n-1}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} with L⊆ML\subseteq M, one has

(3) Vn⁡(L,C1,…,Cn−1)≤Vn⁡(M,C1,…,Cn−1).\operatorname{V}_{n}(L,C_{1},\dots,C_{n-1})\leq\operatorname{V}_{n}(M,C_{1},\dots,C_{n-1}).

Write ι1,ι2:ℝn→(ℝn)2\iota_{1},\iota_{2}:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow(\mathbb{R}^{n})^{2} for the canonical embeddings into the first and second factors, respectively. The body K2=K×K⊆(ℝn)2K^{2}=K\times K\subseteq(\mathbb{R}^{n})^{2} can then be written as K2=ι1​K+ι2​KK^{2}=\iota_{1}K+\iota_{2}K. Denote by Δ:ℝn→(ℝn)2\Delta:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow(\mathbb{R}^{n})^{2} the diagonal embedding given by Δ⁡(x)=(x,x)\Delta(x)=(x,x), x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. Then for any convex body K⊆ℝnK\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} we have Δ​K⊆K2\Delta K\subseteq K^{2} and hence

(4) Vn⁡(K)​Vn​(K⁡[k],−K⁡[n−k])=(2​nn)​V2​n​(Δ​K​[n],ι1​K​[k],ι2​K​[n−k])≤(2​nn)​V2​n​(K2​[n],ι1​K​[k],ι2​K​[n−k])=(nk)​Vn​(K)2,\displaystyle\begin{split}\operatorname{V}_{n}(K)\operatorname{V}_{n}\bigl(K[k],-K[n-k]\bigr)&=\binom{2n}{n}\operatorname{V}_{2n}\bigl(\Delta K[n],\iota_{1}K[k],\iota_{2}K[n-k]\bigr)\\ &\leq\binom{2n}{n}\operatorname{V}_{2n}\bigl(K^{2}[n],\iota_{1}K[k],\iota_{2}K[n-k]\bigr)\\ &=\binom{n}{k}\operatorname{V}_{n}(K)^{2},\end{split}

where the inequality uses (3) nn times and the equalities follow from the standard projection formula for mixed volumes (see [17] and Section 3 below for more details). If KK is full-dimensional, dividing by Vn⁡(K)>0\operatorname{V}_{n}(K)>0 proves (2). In addition, equality in (2) holds if and only if the monotonicity inequalities used in (4) all hold with equality.

It is well known that equality in the monotonicity inequality (3) can be reformulated as a condition in terms of the support of mixed area measures, see Lemma 2.10. In our case, this implies that KK is an extremizer of (4) if and only if the support functions of Δ​K\Delta K and K2K^{2} are equal on the support of certain mixed area measures, more precisely,

(5) hΔ​K=hK2onsupp⁡SB⁡[n−1],ι1​K​[k],ι2​K​[n−k],h_{\Delta K}=h_{K^{2}}\quad\text{on}\quad\operatorname{supp}\operatorname{S}_{B[n-1],\iota_{1}K[k],\iota_{2}K[n-k]},

see Section 2 for notation and more details.

While an explicit characterization of the support of the mixed area measure is a wide open problem in general, it turns out that in this special case, equality in the monotonicity inequality admits a simple geometric interpretation. More precisely, we prove a local version of the aforementioned projection formula, with mixed volumes replaced by mixed area measures (see Proposition 4.3), which allows us to reformulate (5) as a condition on the touching cones of KK (see Section 2.1.2 for definition and more details). These constitute the first step of the proof of Theorem 1.2 and result in the following proposition.

Proposition 1.3.

Let 1≤k≤n−11\leq k\leq n-1. Assume K⊆ℝnK\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} is a full-dimensional convex body. Then KK attains equality in (2) if and only if for any two directions u,v∈ℝnu,v\in\mathbb{R}^{n} with dimT⁡(K,u)≤k\dim T(K,u)\leq k and dimT⁡(K,v)≤n−k\dim T(K,v)\leq n-k, there exists a direction w∈ℝnw\in\mathbb{R}^{n} such that T⁡(K,w)T(K,w) contains both T⁡(K,u)T(K,u) and T⁡(K,v)T(K,v).

Now assume that KK contains the origin in its interior. The fact that touching cones and faces are dual notions under the operation of polarity (see Section 2) then allows us to translate the conclusion in Proposition 1.3 to a condition on the face lattice of the polar body K∘K^{\circ}. This states that for any two faces FF and GG of K∘K^{\circ} with dimF≤k−1\dim F\leq k-1 and dimG≤n−k−1\dim G\leq n-k-1, there exists a proper face of K∘K^{\circ} containing both of them. The second step in our classification of equality cases in (2) is that this face lattice condition already characterizes simplices.

Theorem 1.4.

Let K⊆ℝnK\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} be a full-dimensional convex body and fix an integer 1≤k≤n−11\leq k\leq n-1. The following are equivalent:

  1. (a)

    KK is a simplex.

  2. (b)

    For any two faces FF and GG of KK with dimF≤k−1\dim F\leq k-1 and dimG≤n−k−1\dim G\leq n-k-1, there exists a proper face HH of KK containing both FF and GG.

  3. (c)

    For any two directions u,v∈ℝnu,v\in\mathbb{R}^{n} with dimT⁡(K,u)≤k\dim T(K,u)\leq k and dimT⁡(K,v)≤n−k\dim T(K,v)\leq n-k, there exists a direction w∈ℝnw\in\mathbb{R}^{n} such that T⁡(K,w)T(K,w) contains both T⁡(K,u)T(K,u) and T⁡(K,v)T(K,v).

We remark that Theorem 1.4 establishes a characterization of simplices entirely in terms of their facial or normal structure. The only previous result in this direction known to us is due to Develin [9, Theorem 1], who proved Theorem 1.4 when KK is a polytope. The core difficulty of Theorem 1.4, however, is that the face lattice of a general convex body is possibly infinite. Yet, our proof strategy is motivated by Develin’s argument; more precisely, we inductively reduce the statement to the case k=1k=1 where a simpler direct proof is available.

Theorem 1.2 now follows at once by combining Theorem 1.4 with Proposition 1.3.

1.2. Higher-order Godbersen’s inequality and equality cases

The key insight of the proof of (2) given in [17] and outlined above is the embedding of the problem to the product space. This idea originated in the previous study of a certain natural generalization of Conjecture 1.1 by the first- and second-named authors [16, 11] as we now explain.

For p≥1p\geq 1, let Δp:ℝn→(ℝn)p\Delta_{p}:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to(\mathbb{R}^{n})^{p} be the diagonal map Δp​(x)=(x,…,x)\Delta_{p}(x)=(x,\ldots,x) and let ιi:ℝn→(ℝn)p\iota_{i}:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to(\mathbb{R}^{n})^{p} be the embedding of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} into the ii-th copy of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} in (ℝn)p(\mathbb{R}^{n})^{p}. Then the pp-th Cartesian product of K⊆ℝnK\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} equals Kp=ι1​K+⋯+ιp​KK^{p}=\iota_{1}K+\cdots+\iota_{p}K. We denote by Vp​n\operatorname{V}_{pn} the mixed volume in ℝp​n\mathbb{R}^{pn}. Schneider [24, Satz 2] proved the following higher-order version of the Rogers–Shephard inequality:

(6) Vp​n⁡(Kp−Δp​K)≤(p​n+nn)​Vn​(K)p,\operatorname{V}_{pn}\bigl(K^{p}-\Delta_{p}K\bigr)\leq\binom{pn+n}{n}\operatorname{V}_{n}(K)^{p},

where equality holds if and only if KK is lower-dimensional or a simplex.

Using the multilinearity of mixed volume on the left-hand side of (6) and a suitable Vandermonde expansion of (p​n+nn){pn+n\choose n} on the right, one may again expect that the inequality (6) holds term-wise, with simplices being the only nontrivial extremizers. This higher-order Godbersen inequality was first conjectured by Schneider [26, p. 537] and later independently by the second-named author [16, Conjecture 1.3]. Previous results on this conjecture were essentially limited to the generalization of the known cases of the original Godbersen conjecture to the higher-order setting, with partial contributions by Janson (see [26]), the second-named author [16], and the first- and second-named authors [11].

Our second main result resolves the higher-order Godbersen conjecture in full generality.

Theorem 1.5.

Let p≥1p\geq 1 and 0≤k0,…,kp≤n0\leq k_{0},\dots,k_{p}\leq n be integers such that ∑i=0pki=n\sum_{i=0}^{p}k_{i}=n. For any convex body K⊆ℝnK\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} we have

(7) Vp​n⁡(−Δp​K​[n−k0],ι1​K​[n−k1],…,ιp​K​[n−kp])≤(n!)p(p​n)!​(nk0,…,kp)​Vn​(K)p.\operatorname{V}_{pn}\bigl(-\Delta_{p}K[n-k_{0}],\iota_{1}K[n-k_{1}],\ldots,\iota_{p}K[n-k_{p}]\bigr)\leq\frac{(n!)^{p}}{(pn)!}\binom{n}{k_{0},\ldots,k_{p}}\operatorname{V}_{n}(K)^{p}.

If ki<nk_{i}<n for all ii and KK is full-dimensional, then equality holds if and only if KK is a simplex.

Remark 1.6.

If ki=nk_{i}=n for some ii, then both sides of (7) are equal to (n!)p(p​n)!​Vn​(K)p\frac{(n!)^{p}}{(pn)!}\operatorname{V}_{n}(K)^{p}, see [16, Remark 3.5 (b)], hence equality is attained for any KK. Similarly, if KK is lower-dimensional, then both sides of (7) are always equal to zero.

Furthermore, by [11, Lemma 3.1], zero indices can be eliminated without changing whether equality holds. Thus, apart from the trivial cases above, it suffices to consider k0,…,kp≥1k_{0},\dots,k_{p}\geq 1, which in particular implies p≤n−1p\leq n-1.

Note that for p=1p=1, Theorem 1.5 subsumes the Godbersen inequality (2) and its equality characterization Theorem 1.2. It was pointed out in [17] that the proof of (7) follows from the same monotonicity argument as in the case p=1p=1. We give the proof of the general inequality (7) in Section 3.

The proof of the equality cases of (7) follows a similar strategy as Theorem 1.2. First, we show the following analogue of Proposition 1.3.

Proposition 1.7.

Let 1≤p≤n−11\leq p\leq n-1 and fix integers k0,…,kp≥1k_{0},\dots,k_{p}\geq 1 with ∑i=0pki=n\sum_{i=0}^{p}k_{i}=n. Assume K⊆ℝnK\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} is a full-dimensional convex body. Then KK attains equality in (7) if and only if for any p+1p+1 directions u0,…,up∈ℝnu_{0},\dots,u_{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} with dimT⁡(K,ui)≤ki\dim T(K,u_{i})\leq k_{i}, there exists a direction w∈ℝnw\in\mathbb{R}^{n} such that T⁡(K,ui)⊆T⁡(K,w)T(K,u_{i})\subseteq T(K,w) for all i=0,…,pi=0,\dots,p.

We then inductively extend Theorem 1.4 from two faces (touching cones) to p+1p+1 faces (touching cones) in the following way.

Theorem 1.8.

Let K⊆ℝnK\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} be a full-dimensional convex body. Let 1≤p≤n−11\leq p\leq n-1 and fix integers k0,…,kp≥1k_{0},\ldots,k_{p}\geq 1 with ∑i=0pki=n\sum_{i=0}^{p}k_{i}=n. Then the following are equivalent:

  1. (a)

    KK is a simplex.

  2. (b)

    For any faces F0,…,FpF_{0},\ldots,F_{p} of KK with dimFi≤ki−1\dim F_{i}\leq k_{i}-1, i=0,…,pi=0,\dots,p, there exists a proper face FF of KK such that Fi⊆FF_{i}\subseteq F for all i=0,…,pi=0,\dots,p.

  3. (c)

    For any p+1p+1 directions u0,…,up∈ℝnu_{0},\dots,u_{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} with dimT⁡(K,ui)≤ki\dim T(K,u_{i})\leq k_{i}, i=0,…,pi=0,\dots,p, there exists a direction w∈ℝnw\in\mathbb{R}^{n} such that T⁡(K,ui)⊆T⁡(K,w)T(K,u_{i})\subseteq T(K,w) for all i=0,…,pi=0,\dots,p.

Combining Proposition 1.7 with Theorem 1.8 then completes the equality characterization of the higher-order Godbersen inequality (7), and thus proves Theorem 1.5.

1.3. Relation to other recent work

Brandenberg, González Merino, and Grundbacher [6], using an argument from [17] together with a consequence of (7), previously conjectured in [16, Conjecture 1.2], recently proved an LqL_{q}-version of Schneider’s inequality (6) for general q∈[1,∞]q\in[1,\infty]. Moreover, they also established an optimal stability result for their inequality. This in particular subsumes a stability version of (6), generalizing to the higher-order setting the stability of the Rogers–Shephard inequality previously proven by Böröczky [5].

By the time the present paper was completed, we learned that Friedland, Putterman, and Szusterman [10] also obtained the equality characterization for the Godbersen inequality (2) using an approach significantly different from ours. Notably, their approach is based on using algebraic manipulations to reduce the problem of characterizing equality cases of (2) to the case k=1k=1, where Conjecture 1.1 was known to hold. Although we use a similar reduction scheme to prove Theorem 1.4, our method is more geometric in nature and deals with the equality cases for each k=1,…,n−1k=1,\dots,n-1. In a subsequent update, Friedland, Putterman, and Szusterman [10] extended their approach to the higher-order Godbersen inequality (7), providing another proof of our Theorem 1.5.

Organization of the paper.

Section 2 recalls facial structure, normal structure, mixed volumes, and mixed area measures. Section 3 proves the inequality part in Theorem 1.5. Section 4 proves the local projection formula for mixed area measures, and Propositions 1.3 and 1.7. Section 5 proves Theorem 1.4 and thus together with Section 4 completes the proof of Theorem 1.2. Section 6 proves Theorem 1.8 and combined with Section 4, proves the equality characterization in Theorem 1.5.

2. Preliminaries

A convex body is a nonempty compact convex set, possibly of lower dimension. We denote by 𝒦n\mathcal{K}^{n} the set of all convex bodies in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. Since the polar body is an important tool in this paper, we will often work with the class 𝒦on\mathcal{K}^{n}_{o} of full-dimensional convex bodies in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} containing the origin in their interior. Throughout the paper we assume n≥2n\geq 2.

2.1. Facial and normal structure

We first recall basic notions about the facial structure and normal structure of convex bodies and refer to [27, §2.1–2.2], [20, §18], [33], and [31] for a more comprehensive treatment.

2.1.1. Facial structure

For two points x,y∈ℝnx,y\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, denote by [x,y][x,y] the closed line segment from xx to yy and denote by (x,y)(x,y) the open line segment from xx to yy. A face of a convex body K∈𝒦nK\in\mathcal{K}^{n} is a nonempty convex subset F⊆KF\subseteq K such that, whenever x,y∈Kx,y\in K and (x,y)∩F≠∅(x,y)\cap F\neq\emptyset, the whole segment [x,y][x,y] lies in FF. In particular, KK is a face of itself, and any face other than KK is called a proper face. Note that a face of a face of KK is again a face of KK. Also, if FF and GG are two faces of KK, then F∩GF\cap G, if nonempty, is a face of FF, GG, and KK.

For any nonempty subset A⊆KA\subseteq K, we define F⁡(K,A)F(K,A) as the smallest (in the order of inclusion) face of KK containing AA. Alternatively, F⁡(K,A)=⋂F⊇AFF(K,A)=\bigcap_{F\supseteq A}F, where the intersection runs over all faces FF of KK containing AA. When A={x}A=\{x\} for some x∈Kx\in K, we write simply F⁡(K,x)F(K,x) instead of F⁡(K,{x})F(K,\{x\}).11 1 In previous literature, the notation F⁡(K,u)F(K,u) is often used for the exposed face in the direction of uu. However, we reserve it for general faces since exposed faces are almost never used in the present paper.

Lemma 2.1.

The face F⁡(K,x)F(K,x) is the unique face of KK containing xx in its relative interior.

Proof.

First, we have x∈relint⁡F⁡(K,x)x\in\operatorname{relint}F(K,x). Indeed, if x∈relbd⁡F⁡(K,x)x\in\operatorname{relbd}F(K,x), then we may choose a proper face GG of F⁡(K,x)F(K,x) containing xx. Then GG is a face of KK which is strictly contained in F⁡(K,x)F(K,x), contradicting the definition of F⁡(K,x)F(K,x). Now we show the uniqueness. Let F′F^{\prime} be any face with x∈relint⁡F′x\in\operatorname{relint}F^{\prime}. Then x∈F⁡(K,x)∩F′x\in F(K,x)\cap F^{\prime}. The definition of F⁡(K,x)F(K,x) implies F⁡(K,x)⊆F′F(K,x)\subseteq F^{\prime}. Therefore, F⁡(K,x)F(K,x) is a face of F′F^{\prime}. But if F⁡(K,x)F(K,x) is a proper face of F′F^{\prime}, then x∈F⁡(K,x)⊆relbd⁡F′x\in F(K,x)\subseteq\operatorname{relbd}F^{\prime}, contradicting the choice of F′F^{\prime}. Hence F′=F⁡(K,x)F^{\prime}=F(K,x) as desired. ∎

A point x∈Kx\in K is an extreme point if {x}\{x\} is a face of KK. More generally, a point x∈Kx\in K is called pp-extreme if dimF⁡(K,x)≤p\dim F(K,x)\leq p. In particular, 0-extreme points are exactly extreme points. We recall that Minkowski’s theorem asserts that a convex body is the convex hull of its extreme points [27, Corollary 1.4.5].

Consider the collection of all the faces of KK together with the empty set, ordered by inclusion. This forms a lattice, which we call the face lattice of KK. For two faces F,GF,\,G of KK, their join F∨GF\vee G is therefore the smallest face containing both of them, which may be KK. In other words, F∨G=F⁡(K,F∪G)F\vee G=F(K,F\cup G). Their meet is F∧G=F∩GF\wedge G=F\cap G, which may be empty. When F={x}F=\{x\} is a singleton, we write simply F∨G=x∨GF\vee G=x\vee G.

The support function of a convex body K∈𝒦nK\in\mathcal{K}^{n} is defined by hK​(y):=maxx∈K⁡⟨y,x⟩h_{K}(y):=\max_{x\in K}\langle y,x\rangle, y∈ℝny\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. Observe that hKh_{K} is 1-homogeneous. The exposed face of KK in the direction of u∈𝕊n−1u\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1} is given by {x∈K:⟨u,x⟩=hK​(u)}\{x\in K:\langle u,x\rangle=h_{K}(u)\}. An exposed face is always a face but not vice versa. While this will not be used in the paper, we note that exposed faces together with the empty set also form a lattice.

We record two elementary facts about faces that will be repeatedly used throughout the proof of Theorem 1.4 in Section 5.

Lemma 2.2.

Let FF and GG be faces of K∈𝒦nK\in\mathcal{K}^{n}. If F∩relint⁡G≠∅F\cap\operatorname{relint}G\neq\emptyset, then G⊆FG\subseteq F.

Proof.

Fix x∈F∩relint⁡Gx\in F\cap\operatorname{relint}G. For any a∈G∖{x}a\in G\setminus\{x\}, there exists b∈Gb\in G such that x∈(a,b)x\in(a,b). Since FF is a face, we have a,b∈Fa,b\in F. Since aa was chosen arbitrarily in GG, it follows that G⊆FG\subseteq F. ∎

Lemma 2.3.

Let FF and GG be faces of K∈𝒦nK\in\mathcal{K}^{n}, and let u∈relint⁡Fu\in\operatorname{relint}F and v∈relint⁡Gv\in\operatorname{relint}G. Then (u,v)⊆relint⁡(F∨G)(u,v)\subseteq\operatorname{relint}(F\vee G).

Proof.

Let x∈(u,v)x\in(u,v) and consider H:=F⁡(K,x)H:=F(K,x). Lemma 2.1 implies x∈relint⁡Hx\in\operatorname{relint}H. Since x∈(u,v)x\in(u,v), we have u,v∈Hu,v\in H. Hence by Lemma 2.2 we have F,G⊆HF,G\subseteq H. Since x∈F∨Gx\in F\vee G, we have H=F∨GH=F\vee G. Therefore x∈relint⁡(F∨G)x\in\operatorname{relint}(F\vee G) and the claim follows. ∎

2.1.2. Normal structure and duality

This entire section is dual to Section 2.1.1 under taking the polar body, see below. We first recall normal cones, which are dual to exposed faces. Fix a convex body K∈𝒦nK\in\mathcal{K}^{n}. The normal cone at x∈Kx\in K is

N⁡(K,x):={v∈ℝn:⟨v,y−x⟩≤0​ for every ​y∈K}.N(K,x):=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:\langle v,y-x\rangle\leq 0\text{ for every }y\in K\}.

Second, we recall touching cones, which are dual to faces. For u∈ℝnu\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, fix any x∈Kx\in K with ⟨x,u⟩=hK​(u)\langle x,u\rangle=h_{K}(u) and define the touching cone T⁡(K,u)T(K,u) as the smallest face of N⁡(K,x)N(K,x) containing uu. It can be seen that this does not depend on the choice of xx. In this paper, we consider {0}\{0\} as a touching cone or a normal cone: when KK is full-dimensional, N⁡(K,x)={0}N(K,x)=\{0\} for x∈int⁡Kx\in\interior K and T⁡(K,0)={0}T(K,0)=\{0\}. We call a nonzero touching (normal) cone a proper touching (normal) cone. Lastly, we recall pp-extreme directions, which are dual to pp-extreme points. A direction u∈𝕊n−1u\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1} is called pp-extreme if dimT⁡(K,u)≤p+1\dim T(K,u)\leq p+1.

While normal and touching cones are defined for all convex bodies, in order to introduce the duality we further assume K∈𝒦onK\in\mathcal{K}^{n}_{o}. The polar (dual) body K∘:={v∈ℝn:hK​(v)≤1}K^{\circ}:=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:h_{K}(v)\leq 1\} also belongs to 𝒦on\mathcal{K}^{n}_{o}. The following fact, due to Weis [33], establishes the duality between touching cones (normal cones resp.) of KK and faces (exposed faces resp.) of K∘K^{\circ}.

Lemma 2.4 ([33, Proposition 4.7 and Theorem 8.3]).

Let K∈𝒦onK\in\mathcal{K}^{n}_{o}. There exist bijections

{proper faces of ​K∘}\displaystyle\{\text{proper faces of }K^{\circ}\} ⟶∼​{proper touching cones of ​K},\displaystyle\overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow}\{\text{proper touching cones of }K\},
{proper exposed faces of ​K∘}\displaystyle\{\text{proper exposed faces of }K^{\circ}\} ⟶∼​{proper normal cones of ​K},\displaystyle\overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow}\{\text{proper normal cones of }K\},

given by F↦ℝ≥0​FF\mapsto\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}F. Moreover, the map T↦T∩∂K∘T\mapsto T\cap\partial K^{\circ} gives the inverse to both maps above.

Remark 2.5.

Using the first bijection of Lemma 2.4, we may immediately transfer all the properties of faces to touching cones. For example, Lemma 2.1 implies that u∈relint⁡T⁡(K,u)u\in\operatorname{relint}T(K,u). In addition, for any v∈T⁡(K,u)∖{0}v\in T(K,u)\setminus\{0\}, T⁡(K,v)T(K,v) is the face of T⁡(K,u)T(K,u) containing vv in the relative interior, cf. [31, Lemma 2.2]. Note also that u∈𝕊n−1u\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1} is a pp-extreme direction for K∈𝒦onK\in\mathcal{K}^{n}_{o} if and only if ℝ≥0​u∩∂K∘\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}u\cap\partial K^{\circ} is a pp-extreme point of K∘K^{\circ}.

Finally, we recall the relation between the touching cones of a projection with the touching cones of the original body. Write TET_{E} for the cones computed in a subspace E⊆ℝnE\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}. If u∈E∩𝕊n−1u\in E\cap\mathbb{S}^{n-1}, then

(8) TE​(PE⁡K,u)=T⁡(K,u)∩E,\displaystyle T_{E}(\operatorname{P}_{E}K,u)=T(K,u)\cap E,

where PE:ℝn→E\operatorname{P}_{E}:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to E is the orthogonal projection. This follows by applying [31, Lemma 2.4] iteratively.

2.2. Mixed volumes and mixed area measures

Now we define mixed volumes and mixed area measures, and recall their properties which will be needed in later sections. The standard reference for this material is [27, Chapter 5].

For convex bodies K1,…,Km∈𝒦nK_{1},\dots,K_{m}\in\mathcal{K}^{n} and t1,…,tm≥0t_{1},\dots,t_{m}\geq 0, the volume

Vn(∑i=1mtiKi)=∑i1,…,in=1mti1⋯tinVn(Ki1,…,Kin)\operatorname{V}_{n}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}t_{i}K_{i}\right)=\sum_{i_{1},\dots,i_{n}=1}^{m}t_{i_{1}}\cdots t_{i_{n}}\operatorname{V}_{n}(K_{i_{1}},\dots,K_{i_{n}})

is a homogeneous polynomial whose symmetric coefficients Vn⁡(Ki1,…,Kin)\operatorname{V}_{n}(K_{i_{1}},\dots,K_{i_{n}}) are called mixed volumes. Mixed volumes are nonnegative, translation invariant, and multilinear. Volume can be recovered from mixed volumes by Vn⁡(K)=Vn⁡(K⁡[n])\operatorname{V}_{n}(K)=\operatorname{V}_{n}(K[n]), where K⁡[r]K[r] denotes rr repeated copies of KK. More generally, when the convex bodies are contained in a subspace E⊆ℝnE\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}, we write VdimEE\operatorname{V}_{\dim E}^{E} for volume and mixed volume computed within EE. In particular, Vn=Vnℝn\operatorname{V}_{n}=\operatorname{V}_{n}^{\mathbb{R}^{n}}.

It is easily seen from the definition that mixed volumes are affine covariant: for any affine map ϕ:ℝn→ℝn\phi:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n}, where ϕ⁡(x)=A​x+b\phi(x)=Ax+b, and bodies K1,…,Kn∈𝒦nK_{1},\dots,K_{n}\in\mathcal{K}^{n}, we have

(9) Vn⁡(ϕ​K1,…,ϕ​Kn)=|detA|​Vn​(K1,…,Kn).\operatorname{V}_{n}(\phi K_{1},\dots,\phi K_{n})=|\det A|\operatorname{V}_{n}(K_{1},\dots,K_{n}).

We also recall the projection formula for mixed volumes [27, Theorem 5.3.1]. Let E⊆ℝnE\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} be a kk-dimensional subspace, where 1≤k≤n−11\leq k\leq n-1. Then for any L1,…,Lk,M1,…,Mn−k∈𝒦nL_{1},\dots,L_{k},M_{1},\dots,M_{n-k}\in\mathcal{K}^{n} with Li⊆EL_{i}\subseteq E for i=1,…,ki=1,\dots,k, one has

(10) (nk)​Vn​(L1,…,Lk,M1,…,Mn−k)=VkE⁡(L1,…,Lk)​Vn−kE⟂​(PE⟂⁡M1,…,PE⟂⁡Mn−k).\binom{n}{k}\operatorname{V}_{n}(L_{1},\dots,L_{k},M_{1},\dots,M_{n-k})=\operatorname{V}_{k}^{E}(L_{1},\dots,L_{k})\operatorname{V}_{n-k}^{E^{\perp}}(\operatorname{P}_{E^{\perp}}M_{1},\dots,\operatorname{P}_{E^{\perp}}M_{n-k}).

We will also need a similar formula for multiple linearly independent subspaces.

Lemma 2.6.

Let E1,…,Em⊆ℝnE_{1},\dots,E_{m}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} be linearly independent subspaces with di:=dimEi≥1d_{i}:=\dim E_{i}\geq 1 and ∑i=1mdi=n\sum_{i=1}^{m}d_{i}=n. For convex bodies Ki⊆EiK_{i}\subseteq E_{i}, one has

(11) (nd1,…,dm)​Vn​(K1​[d1],…,Km​[dm])=|detT|​∏i=1mVdiEi⁡(Ki),\displaystyle\binom{n}{d_{1},\dots,d_{m}}\operatorname{V}_{n}(K_{1}[d_{1}],\dots,K_{m}[d_{m}])=|\det T|\prod_{i=1}^{m}\operatorname{V}_{d_{i}}^{E_{i}}(K_{i}),

where T:ℝn→⨁i=1mEiT:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\bigoplus_{i=1}^{m}E_{i} is given by T​x=(PEi⁡x)i=1mTx=(\operatorname{P}_{E_{i}}x)_{i=1}^{m}.

Proof.

By (9), for t1,…,tm≥0t_{1},\dots,t_{m}\geq 0 we have

Vn⁡(∑i=1mti​Ki)=|detT|​∏i=1mtidi​VdiEi⁡(Ki).\operatorname{V}_{n}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}t_{i}K_{i}\right)=|\det T|\prod_{i=1}^{m}t_{i}^{d_{i}}\operatorname{V}_{d_{i}}^{E_{i}}(K_{i}).

Comparing the coefficients of t1d1⋯tmdmt_{1}^{d_{1}}\cdots t_{m}^{d_{m}} proves the claim. ∎

For convex bodies C1,…,Cn−1∈𝒦nC_{1},\dots,C_{n-1}\in\mathcal{K}^{n}, their mixed area measure SC1,…,Cn−1\operatorname{S}_{C_{1},\dots,C_{n-1}} is defined as the unique measure on 𝕊n−1\mathbb{S}^{n-1} such that

(12) Vn⁡(K,C1,…,Cn−1)=1n​∫𝕊n−1hK​d​SC1,…,Cn−1\operatorname{V}_{n}(K,C_{1},\dots,C_{n-1})=\frac{1}{n}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}h_{K}d\operatorname{S}_{C_{1},\dots,C_{n-1}}

holds for all K∈𝒦nK\in\mathcal{K}^{n}. Similar to mixed volumes, mixed area measures are nonnegative, translation invariant, and multilinear. When the bodies C1,…,Cd−1C_{1},\dots,C_{d-1} are contained in a dd-dimensional subspace E⊆ℝnE\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}, we will denote the mixed area measure by SC1,…,Cd−1E\operatorname{S}^{E}_{C_{1},\ldots,C_{d-1}} to specify the ambient space.

By (9), mixed area measures satisfy the following covariance formula under invertible linear maps, cf. [27, Equation (5.24)]. For any invertible linear map A:ℝn→ℝnA:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{n}, convex bodies C1,…,Cn−1∈𝒦nC_{1},\dots,C_{n-1}\in\mathcal{K}^{n}, and any continuous positively 11-homogeneous function f:ℝn→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}, we have

(13) ∫𝕊n−1f⁡(v)​d​SA​C1,…,A​Cn−1⁡(v)=|detA|​∫𝕊n−1f⁡(A−t​u)​d​SC1,…,Cn−1⁡(u),\int_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}f(v)\,d\operatorname{S}_{AC_{1},\dots,AC_{n-1}}(v)=|\det A|\int_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}f(A^{-t}u)\,d\operatorname{S}_{C_{1},\dots,C_{n-1}}(u),

where A−tA^{-t} denotes the inverse transpose of AA.

2.2.1. Mixed discriminants

For convex bodies with C2C^{2} support functions, the mixed area measure admits an explicit representation in terms of mixed discriminants. Denote by Sym⁡(n)\Sym(n) the set of symmetric nn-by-nn matrices. The mixed discriminant Dn\operatorname{D}_{n} is defined as the unique symmetric multilinear function on Sym⁡(n)n\Sym(n)^{n} such that Dn⁡(M,…,M)=det(M)\operatorname{D}_{n}(M,\dots,M)=\det(M) holds for all M∈Sym⁡(n)M\in\operatorname{Sym(n)}. Now, for Ci∈𝒦nC_{i}\in\mathcal{K}^{n} such that hCi∈C2​(𝕊n−1)h_{C_{i}}\in C^{2}(\mathbb{S}^{n-1}), their mixed area measure has a density with respect to the Hausdorff measure on the sphere 𝕊n−1\mathbb{S}^{n-1}; see [27, Equation (2.68)]. More precisely, for u∈𝕊n−1u\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1}, one has

(14) d​SC1,…,Cn−1d​ℋn−1​(u)=Dn−1⁡(D2​hC1​(u),…,D2​hCn−1​(u)),\frac{d\operatorname{S}_{C_{1},\dots,C_{n-1}}}{d\mathcal{H}^{n-1}}(u)=\operatorname{D}_{n-1}(D^{2}h_{C_{1}}(u),\dots,D^{2}h_{C_{n-1}}(u)),

where D2​hC∈Sym⁡(n−1)D^{2}h_{C}\in\Sym(n-1) is the restriction of the Euclidean Hessian of hCh_{C} to u⟂u^{\perp}.

We will need the following version of Lemma 2.6 for mixed discriminants.

Lemma 2.7.

Let E1,…,Em⊆ℝnE_{1},\dots,E_{m}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} be linearly independent subspaces with di:=dimEi≥1d_{i}:=\dim E_{i}\geq 1 and ∑i=1mdi=n\sum_{i=1}^{m}d_{i}=n. For any symmetric matrices A1,…,Am∈Sym⁡(n)A_{1},\dots,A_{m}\in\Sym(n) such that AiA_{i} vanishes on Ei⟂E_{i}^{\perp}, i=1,…,mi=1,\dots,m, one has

(15) (nd1,…,dm)​Dn​(A1​[d1],…,Am​[dm])=|detT|2​∏i=1mdet(Ai|Ei),\binom{n}{d_{1},\ldots,d_{m}}\operatorname{D}_{n}(A_{1}[d_{1}],\ldots,A_{m}[d_{m}])=|\det T|^{2}\prod_{i=1}^{m}\det(A_{i}|_{E_{i}}),

where T:ℝn→⨁i=1mEiT:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\bigoplus_{i=1}^{m}E_{i} is given by T​x=(PEi​x)i=1mTx=(P_{E_{i}}x)_{i=1}^{m}.

Proof.

The operator TT block diagonalizes ∑i=1mti​Ai\sum_{i=1}^{m}t_{i}A_{i} for any t1,…,tm∈ℝt_{1},\dots,t_{m}\in\mathbb{R}. Hence

det(∑i=1mti​Ai)=det(Tt​diag⁡(ti​Ai|Ei)i=1m​T)=|detT|2​∏i=1mtidi​det(Ai|Ei),\det\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}t_{i}A_{i}\right)=\det\left(T^{t}\operatorname{diag}(t_{i}A_{i}|_{E_{i}})_{i=1}^{m}T\right)=|\det T|^{2}\prod_{i=1}^{m}t_{i}^{d_{i}}\det(A_{i}|_{E_{i}}),

where diag⁡(ti​Ai|Ei)i=1m\operatorname{diag}(t_{i}A_{i}|_{E_{i}})_{i=1}^{m} is the block diagonal matrix where the ii-th block is ti​Ai|Eit_{i}A_{i}|_{E_{i}}. The conclusion now follows by comparing coefficients. ∎

In Section 4.1, we will see that (15) gives rise, via (14), to a local projection formula for mixed area measures.

2.2.2. Monotonicity of mixed volumes and support of mixed area measures

Using the representation of mixed volumes by mixed area measures (12), we immediately obtain the monotonicity inequality for mixed volumes: for K,L∈𝒦nK,L\in\mathcal{K}^{n} with K⊆LK\subseteq L, we have hK≤hLh_{K}\leq h_{L} and hence

Vn⁡(K,C1,…,Cn−1)≤Vn⁡(L,C1,…,Cn−1),\operatorname{V}_{n}(K,C_{1},\dots,C_{n-1})\leq\operatorname{V}_{n}(L,C_{1},\dots,C_{n-1}),

and equality holds if and only if

hK=hLonsupp⁡SC1,…,Cn−1.h_{K}=h_{L}\quad\text{on}\quad\operatorname{supp}\operatorname{S}_{C_{1},\dots,C_{n-1}}.

This will later be generalized in Lemma 2.10.

Therefore, the study of equality cases in the monotonicity inequality is the same as the study of support of mixed area measures. Schneider [25] made an insightful conjecture which connects the support of mixed area measures to touching cones. Fix C1,…,Cn−1∈𝒦nC_{1},\dots,C_{n-1}\in\mathcal{K}^{n}. We say u∈𝕊n−1u\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1} is a (C1,…,Cn−1)(C_{1},\dots,C_{n-1})-extreme direction if for every I⊆{1,…,n−1}I\subseteq\{1,\dots,n-1\}, we have

dim(∑i∈IT​(Ci,u)⟂)≥|I|.\dim\left(\sum_{i\in I}T(C_{i},u)^{\perp}\right)\geq|I|.

Schneider conjectured that

supp⁡SC1,…,Cn−1=cl⁡{u∈𝕊n−1:u​ is (C1,…,Cn−1)-extreme}.\operatorname{supp}S_{C_{1},\dots,C_{n-1}}=\operatorname{cl}\left\{u\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1}:u\text{ is $(C_{1},\dots,C_{n-1})$-extreme}\right\}.

When C1=⋯=Cn−1=CC_{1}=\cdots=C_{n-1}=C, SC:=SC,…,CS_{C}:=S_{C,\dots,C} is the surface area measure of CC and the (C,…,C)(C,\dots,C)-extreme directions are precisely the 0-extreme directions of CC. It is known that Schneider’s conjecture indeed holds for this case, see [27, Theorem 4.5.3]. However, in general this conjecture is still wide open.

For our purposes, we will need the following partial result from [31, Theorem 1.21]: if K,C1,…,Cn−2∈𝒦nK,C_{1},\ldots,C_{n-2}\in\mathcal{K}^{n}, u∈𝕊n−1u\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1}, dimT⁡(K,u)=1\dim T(K,u)=1, and v∈T​(K,u)⟂∖{0}v\in T(K,u)^{\perp}\setminus\{0\}, then

u∈supp⁡SPv⟂⁡C1,…,Pv⟂⁡Cn−2v⟂⟹u∈supp⁡SK,C1,…,Cn−2.u\in\operatorname{supp}\operatorname{S}^{v^{\perp}}_{\operatorname{P}_{v^{\perp}}C_{1},\ldots,\operatorname{P}_{v^{\perp}}C_{n-2}}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad u\in\operatorname{supp}\operatorname{S}_{K,C_{1},\ldots,C_{n-2}}.

More precisely, we will make use of the following corollary of this result.

Corollary 2.8.

Let E⊆ℝnE\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} be an mm-dimensional subspace, where 2≤m≤n2\leq m\leq n, and let C1,…,Cm−1∈𝒦nC_{1},\dots,C_{m-1}\in\mathcal{K}^{n}. Let BB be the Euclidean unit ball in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. We have

supp⁡SPE⁡C1,…,PE⁡Cm−1E⊆supp⁡SB⁡[n−m],C1,…,Cm−1.\operatorname{supp}\operatorname{S}^{E}_{\operatorname{P}_{E}C_{1},\dots,\operatorname{P}_{E}C_{m-1}}\subseteq\operatorname{supp}\operatorname{S}_{B[n-m],C_{1},\dots,C_{m-1}}.
Proof.

We induct on n−mn-m, the case n=mn=m being immediate. Suppose n>mn>m and fix u∈supp⁡SPE⁡C1,…,PE⁡Cm−1Eu\in\operatorname{supp}\operatorname{S}^{E}_{\operatorname{P}_{E}C_{1},\dots,\operatorname{P}_{E}C_{m-1}}. Choose a unit vector v∈E⟂v\in E^{\perp}. Since Pv⟂⁡B\operatorname{P}_{v^{\perp}}B is the unit ball in v⟂v^{\perp} and PE⁡Pv⟂=PE\operatorname{P}_{E}\operatorname{P}_{v^{\perp}}=\operatorname{P}_{E}, the induction hypothesis gives

u∈supp⁡S(Pv⟂⁡B)​[n−m−1],Pv⟂⁡C1,…,Pv⟂⁡Cm−1v⟂.u\in\operatorname{supp}\operatorname{S}^{v^{\perp}}_{(\operatorname{P}_{v^{\perp}}B)[n-m-1],\operatorname{P}_{v^{\perp}}C_{1},\dots,\operatorname{P}_{v^{\perp}}C_{m-1}}.

Since T⁡(B,u)=ℝ≥0​uT(B,u)=\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}u and v⟂uv\perp u, [31, Theorem  1.21] implies u∈supp⁡SB⁡[n−m],C1,…,Cm−1u\in\operatorname{supp}\operatorname{S}_{B[n-m],C_{1},\dots,C_{m-1}}. ∎

2.2.3. Equality in monotonicity inequality

We recall the following well-known reformulation of the equality cases of the Alexandrov–Fenchel inequality, see [27, Theorem 7.4.2] or [29, Lemma 3.12(a)].

Lemma 2.9.

Let K,L,C1,…,Cn−2∈𝒦nK,L,C_{1},\dots,C_{n-2}\in\mathcal{K}^{n}. Assume Vn⁡(L,L,C1,…,Cn−2)>0\operatorname{V}_{n}(L,L,C_{1},\dots,C_{n-2})>0 and

Vn⁡(K,L,C1,…,Cn−2)2=Vn⁡(K,K,C1,…,Cn−2)​Vn​(L,L,C1,…,Cn−2).\operatorname{V}_{n}(K,L,C_{1},\dots,C_{n-2})^{2}=\operatorname{V}_{n}(K,K,C_{1},\dots,C_{n-2})\operatorname{V}_{n}(L,L,C_{1},\dots,C_{n-2}).

Then SK,C1,…,Cn−2=α​SL,C1,…,Cn−2\operatorname{S}_{K,C_{1},\dots,C_{n-2}}=\alpha\operatorname{S}_{L,C_{1},\dots,C_{n-2}} holds with α=Vn⁡(K,L,C1,…,Cn−2)Vn⁡(L,L,C1,…,Cn−2).\alpha=\frac{\operatorname{V}_{n}(K,L,C_{1},\dots,C_{n-2})}{\operatorname{V}_{n}(L,L,C_{1},\dots,C_{n-2})}.

By iterating this lemma, we obtain a characterization of the monotonicity inequality in terms of the support of mixed area measures in the following lemma, which is [27, Theorem 7.4.6]. We include a more direct proof here for self-containedness.

Lemma 2.10.

Fix an integer 1≤k≤n1\leq k\leq n. Let K,L,C1,…,Cn−k∈𝒦nK,L,C_{1},\dots,C_{n-k}\in\mathcal{K}^{n} be convex bodies such that K⊆LK\subseteq L and Vn⁡(L⁡[k],C1,…,Cn−k)>0\operatorname{V}_{n}(L[k],C_{1},\dots,C_{n-k})>0. Denote by BB the unit Euclidean ball in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. Then

Vn⁡(K⁡[k],C1,…,Cn−k)=Vn⁡(L⁡[k],C1,…,Cn−k)\operatorname{V}_{n}(K[k],C_{1},\ldots,C_{n-k})=\operatorname{V}_{n}(L[k],C_{1},\ldots,C_{n-k})

holds if and only if

hK=hLonsupp⁡SB⁡[k−1],C1,…,Cn−k.h_{K}=h_{L}\quad\text{on}\quad\operatorname{supp}\operatorname{S}_{B[k-1],C_{1},\ldots,C_{n-k}}.
Proof.

We first show the “only if” part by induction on kk. The base case is k=1k=1. By (12),

Vn⁡(K,C1,…,Cn−1)−Vn⁡(L,C1,…,Cn−1)=1n​∫𝕊n−1(hK−hL)​d​SC1,…,Cn−1.\operatorname{V}_{n}(K,C_{1},\dots,C_{n-1})-\operatorname{V}_{n}(L,C_{1},\dots,C_{n-1})=\frac{1}{n}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}(h_{K}-h_{L})d\operatorname{S}_{C_{1},\dots,C_{n-1}}.

Since K⊆LK\subseteq L, we have hK≤hLh_{K}\leq h_{L}. Therefore, the difference on the left-hand side vanishes if and only if hK=hLh_{K}=h_{L} on supp⁡SC1,…,Cn−1\operatorname{supp}\operatorname{S}_{C_{1},\dots,C_{n-1}}.

Now assume the conclusion holds for k−1k-1 and write 𝒞\mathcal{C} for the tuple (C1,…,Cn−k)(C_{1},\dots,C_{n-k}). By assumption and monotonicity of mixed volumes, we have that for all 1≤i≤k−11\leq i\leq k-1, Vn⁡(K⁡[i],L⁡[k−i],𝒞)\operatorname{V}_{n}(K[i],L[k-i],\mathcal{C}) is equal to the same positive constant. In particular,

Vn\displaystyle\operatorname{V}_{n} (K,L,K⁡[i−1],L⁡[k−i−1],𝒞)2\displaystyle(K,L,K[i-1],L[k-i-1],\mathcal{C})^{2}
=Vn⁡(K,K,K⁡[i−1],L⁡[k−i−1],𝒞)​Vn​(L,L,K⁡[i−1],L⁡[k−i−1],𝒞).\displaystyle=\operatorname{V}_{n}(K,K,K[i-1],L[k-i-1],\mathcal{C})\operatorname{V}_{n}(L,L,K[i-1],L[k-i-1],\mathcal{C}).

By Lemma 2.9, this implies SK,K⁡[i−1],L⁡[k−i−1],𝒞=SL,K⁡[i−1],L⁡[k−i−1],𝒞\operatorname{S}_{K,K[i-1],L[k-i-1],\mathcal{C}}=\operatorname{S}_{L,K[i-1],L[k-i-1],\mathcal{C}}, and so by (12) we have

Vn⁡(K⁡[i],L⁡[k−i−1],𝒞,B)=Vn⁡(K⁡[i−1],L⁡[k−i],𝒞,B).\operatorname{V}_{n}(K[i],L[k-i-1],\mathcal{C},B)=\operatorname{V}_{n}(K[i-1],L[k-i],\mathcal{C},B).

Since this holds for all 1≤i≤k−11\leq i\leq k-1, we obtain Vn⁡(K⁡[k−1],𝒞,B)=Vn⁡(L⁡[k−1],𝒞,B)\operatorname{V}_{n}(K[k-1],\mathcal{C},B)=\operatorname{V}_{n}(L[k-1],\mathcal{C},B), and hence, by induction hypothesis,

hK=hLonsupp⁡SB⁡[k−2],𝒞,B=supp⁡SB⁡[k−1],𝒞.h_{K}=h_{L}\quad\text{on}\quad\operatorname{supp}\operatorname{S}_{B[k-2],\mathcal{C},B}=\operatorname{supp}\operatorname{S}_{B[k-1],\mathcal{C}}.

For the “if” part, recall the following classical fact from [27, Lemma 7.6.15]:

supp⁡SC1,C2,…,Cn−1⊆supp⁡SB,C2,…,Cn−1.\operatorname{supp}S_{C_{1},C_{2},\dots,C_{n-1}}\subseteq\operatorname{supp}S_{B,C_{2},\dots,C_{n-1}}.

This together with the assumption implies

Vn⁡(K⁡[k],𝒞)=Vn⁡(K⁡[k−1],L,𝒞).\operatorname{V}_{n}(K[k],\mathcal{C})=\operatorname{V}_{n}(K[k-1],L,\mathcal{C}).

Iterating the same argument then yields Vn⁡(K⁡[k],𝒞)=Vn⁡(L⁡[k],𝒞)\operatorname{V}_{n}(K[k],\mathcal{C})=\operatorname{V}_{n}(L[k],\mathcal{C}). ∎

3. Proof of higher-order Godbersen inequality

We start by proving the higher-order Godbersen inequality (7). The method is essentially the same as the monotonicity argument used in [17] to prove the case p=1p=1.

Proposition 3.1.

Let p≥1p\geq 1 and 0≤k0,…,kp≤n0\leq k_{0},\dots,k_{p}\leq n be integers such that ∑i=0pki=n\sum_{i=0}^{p}k_{i}=n. For any K∈𝒦nK\in\mathcal{K}^{n} we have

(16) Vp​n⁡(−Δp​K​[n−k0],ι1​K​[n−k1],…,ιp​K​[n−kp])≤(n!)p(p​n)!​(nk0,…,kp)​Vn​(K)p.\operatorname{V}_{pn}\bigl(-\Delta_{p}K[n-k_{0}],\iota_{1}K[n-k_{1}],\ldots,\iota_{p}K[n-k_{p}]\bigr)\leq\frac{(n!)^{p}}{(pn)!}\binom{n}{k_{0},\ldots,k_{p}}\operatorname{V}_{n}(K)^{p}.
Proof.

If Vn⁡(K)=0\operatorname{V}_{n}(K)=0, then both sides of (16) are equal to zero. We may thus assume Vn⁡(K)>0\operatorname{V}_{n}(K)>0. For brevity, we will denote N:=(p+1)​nN:=(p+1)n. Let ι~0,…,ι~p:ℝn→ℝN\widetilde{\iota}_{0},\dots,\widetilde{\iota}_{p}:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{N} be the canonical inclusions. Write ℝN=ℝn×ℝp​n\mathbb{R}^{N}=\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}^{pn} and denote by π:ℝN→ℝp​n\pi:\mathbb{R}^{N}\to\mathbb{R}^{pn} the projection to the second factor. Consider further the linear map Φ:ℝN→ℝN\Phi:\mathbb{R}^{N}\to\mathbb{R}^{N} given by

Φ⁡(x0,…,xp):=(x0,x1+x0,…,xp+x0).\Phi(x_{0},\dots,x_{p}):=(x_{0},x_{1}+x_{0},\dots,x_{p}+x_{0}).

Then we have detΦ=1\det\Phi=1 and Φ−1​(x0,…,xp)=(x0,x1−x0,…,xp−x0)\Phi^{-1}(x_{0},\dots,x_{p})=(x_{0},x_{1}-x_{0},\dots,x_{p}-x_{0}). Moreover,

Φ∘ι~0=Δp+1,π∘Φ−1∘ι~0=−Δp,andπ∘Φ−1∘ι~l=ιl,l=1,…,p.\Phi\circ\widetilde{\iota}_{0}=\Delta_{p+1},\qquad\pi\circ\Phi^{-1}\circ\widetilde{\iota}_{0}=-\Delta_{p},\qquad\text{and}\qquad\pi\circ\Phi^{-1}\circ\widetilde{\iota}_{l}=\iota_{l},\quad l=1,\dots,p.

Consequently, (9) and (10) yield

(17) VN⁡(Δp+1​K​[n],ι~0​K​[n−k0],…,ι~p​K​[n−kp])=VN⁡(Φ⁡(ι~0​K)​[n],ι~0​K​[n−k0],…,ι~p​K​[n−kp])=VN⁡(ι~0​K​[n],Φ−1​(ι~0​K)​[n−k0],…,Φ−1​(ι~p​K)​[n−kp])=(Nn)−1​Vn⁡(K)​Vp​n​(−Δp​K​[n−k0],ι1​K​[n−k1],…,ιp​K​[n−kp]).\displaystyle\begin{split}&\operatorname{V}_{N}\big(\Delta_{p+1}K[n],\widetilde{\iota}_{0}K[n-k_{0}],\dots,\widetilde{\iota}_{p}K[n-k_{p}]\big)\\ &\quad=\operatorname{V}_{N}\big(\Phi(\widetilde{\iota}_{0}K)[n],\widetilde{\iota}_{0}K[n-k_{0}],\dots,\widetilde{\iota}_{p}K[n-k_{p}]\big)\\ &\quad=\operatorname{V}_{N}\left(\widetilde{\iota}_{0}K[n],\Phi^{-1}(\widetilde{\iota}_{0}K)[n-k_{0}],\dots,\Phi^{-1}(\widetilde{\iota}_{p}K)[n-k_{p}]\right)\\ &\quad={N\choose n}^{-1}\operatorname{V}_{n}(K)\,\operatorname{V}_{pn}\big(-\Delta_{p}K[n-k_{0}],\iota_{1}K[n-k_{1}],\dots,\iota_{p}K[n-k_{p}]\big).\end{split}

On the other hand, using the monotonicity of mixed volumes, Kp+1=∑l=0pι~l​KK^{p+1}=\sum_{l=0}^{p}\widetilde{\iota}_{l}K, and Lemma 2.6, we have

(18) VN⁡(Δp+1​K​[n],ι~0​K​[n−k0],…,ι~p​K​[n−kp])≤VN⁡(Kp+1​[n],ι~0​K​[n−k0],…,ι~p​K​[n−kp])=(nk0,…,kp)​VN​(ι~0​K​[n],…,ι~p​K​[n])=(nk0,…,kp)​(n!)p+1N!​Vn​(K)p+1.\displaystyle\begin{split}&\operatorname{V}_{N}\big(\Delta_{p+1}K[n],\widetilde{\iota}_{0}K[n-k_{0}],\dots,\widetilde{\iota}_{p}K[n-k_{p}]\big)\\ &\quad\leq\operatorname{V}_{N}\big(K^{p+1}[n],\widetilde{\iota}_{0}K[n-k_{0}],\dots,\widetilde{\iota}_{p}K[n-k_{p}]\big)\\ &\quad={n\choose k_{0},\dots,k_{p}}\operatorname{V}_{N}\big(\widetilde{\iota}_{0}K[n],\dots,\widetilde{\iota}_{p}K[n]\big)\\ &\quad={n\choose k_{0},\dots,k_{p}}\frac{(n!)^{p+1}}{N!}\operatorname{V}_{n}(K)^{p+1}.\end{split}

Since Vn⁡(K)>0\operatorname{V}_{n}(K)>0, (16) follows at once by comparing (17) and (18). ∎

4. Reduction to the face lattice condition

In this section we prove Proposition 1.7 which subsumes Proposition 1.3 as a special case. We first prove the local projection formula and then use the support of mixed area measures to obtain the face lattice condition in Proposition 1.7. Since mixed volumes are translation invariant and KK is assumed to be full-dimensional in Theorem 1.2, we always assume K∈𝒦onK\in\mathcal{K}^{n}_{o}.

4.1. The local projection formula for mixed area measures

In order to prove a local version of the projection formula (11), we will need two simple lemmas.

Lemma 4.1.

For nonzero u,v∈ℝnu,v\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, we have

|det(Pu⟂|v⟂)|=|⟨u,v⟩|‖u‖​‖v‖.\left|\det\left(P_{u^{\perp}}|_{v^{\perp}}\right)\right|=\frac{|\langle u,v\rangle|}{\|u\|\|v\|}.
Proof.

We may assume uu and vv are not parallel, otherwise the claim is trivial. Decompose ℝn=span⁡(u,v)⊕(u⟂∩v⟂)\mathbb{R}^{n}=\operatorname{span}(u,v)\oplus(u^{\perp}\cap v^{\perp}). The projection Pu⟂|v⟂P_{u^{\perp}}|_{v^{\perp}} is the identity on u⟂∩v⟂u^{\perp}\cap v^{\perp} while for x∈v⟂∩span⁡(u,v)x\in v^{\perp}\cap\operatorname{span}(u,v) we have ‖Pu⟂​x‖=|⟨u,v⟩|‖u‖​‖v‖​‖x‖\|P_{u^{\perp}}x\|=\frac{|\langle u,v\rangle|}{\|u\|\|v\|}\|x\|. Therefore, |det(Pu⟂|v⟂)|=|⟨u,v⟩|‖u‖​‖v‖\left|\det\left(P_{u^{\perp}}|_{v^{\perp}}\right)\right|=\frac{|\langle u,v\rangle|}{\|u\|\|v\|}. ∎

5. The two face characterization of simplices

In this section we prove Theorem 1.4 by inductively reducing the incidence condition (b) to the case k=1k=1. This will complete the proof of Theorem 1.2 through Proposition 1.3.

Throughout the section, we write aff⁡(A,B):=aff⁡(A∪B)\operatorname{aff}(A,B):=\operatorname{aff}(A\cup B) and conv⁡(A,B):=conv⁡(A∪B)\operatorname{conv}(A,B):=\operatorname{conv}(A\cup B) for the affine and convex hull, respectively, of nonempty sets A,B⊆ℝnA,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}. Moreover, when B={x}B=\{x\} is a singleton, we write simply conv⁡(A,x)\operatorname{conv}(A,x) instead of conv⁡(A,{x})\operatorname{conv}(A,\{x\}). Since we will repeatedly work with the condition (b) of Theorem 1.4, it will be convenient to capture it by a definition.

Definition 5.1.

Let K∈𝒦nK\in\mathcal{K}^{n}, and let p,q≥0p,q\geq 0 be integers. We say that KK satisfies property (Ip,q)(I_{p,q}) if for any two faces FF and GG of KK with dimF≤p\dim F\leq p and dimG≤q\dim G\leq q, the face F∨GF\vee G is proper.

5.1. Induction on kk

We will show that any K∈𝒦nK\in\mathcal{K}^{n} with property (Ik−1,n−k−1)(I_{k-1,n-k-1}), where 2≤k≤n−12\leq k\leq n-1, also satisfies (Ik−2,n−k)(I_{k-2,n-k}). More precisely, we assume that for any faces FF and GG with dimF≤k−1\dim F\leq k-1 and dimG≤n−k−1\dim G\leq n-k-1, F∨GF\vee G is a proper face. We will show that under this assumption, for any faces FF and GG with dimF≤k−2\dim F\leq k-2 and dimG≤n−k\dim G\leq n-k, F∨GF\vee G is a proper face. Note that we are imposing a stronger dimension condition on FF and a weaker dimension condition on GG.

The key observation for the induction step is that any proper face G′G^{\prime} of GG has dimension at most dimG−1≤n−k−1\dim G-1\leq n-k-1, which allows one to apply (Ik−1,n−k−1)(I_{k-1,n-k-1}) to FF and G′G^{\prime}. This gives a proper face F∨G′F\vee G^{\prime} containing FF and meeting GG. The difficulty here is that, a priori, one has no control on the dimension of F∨G′F\vee G^{\prime}. Therefore, dim(F∨G′)\dim(F\vee G^{\prime}) can take any value between dimF\dim F and n−1n-1. The following lemma deals with the case where dim(F∨G′)≤k−1\dim(F\vee G^{\prime})\leq k-1 by taking T=F∨G′T=F\vee G^{\prime}.

Lemma 5.2.

Suppose that K∈𝒦nK\in\mathcal{K}^{n} satisfies (Ik−1,n−k−1)(I_{k-1,n-k-1}), where 1≤k≤n−11\leq k\leq n-1. Let FF and GG be faces of KK with dimG=n−k\dim G=n-k. If there is a face TT of KK such that F⊆TF\subseteq T, dimT≤k−1\dim T\leq k-1, and T∩G≠∅T\cap G\neq\emptyset, then F∨GF\vee G is proper.

Proof.

Assume such TT exists. If T∩relint⁡G≠∅T\cap\operatorname{relint}G\neq\emptyset, then G⊆TG\subseteq T by Lemma 2.2, and the conclusion follows. Otherwise, choose y∈T∩relbd⁡Gy\in T\cap\operatorname{relbd}G and g∈relint⁡Gg\in\operatorname{relint}G. Then there exists z∈relbd⁡Gz\in\operatorname{relbd}G such that g∈(y,z)g\in(y,z). Since z∈relbd⁡Gz\in\operatorname{relbd}G, F⁡(K,z)F(K,z) is a proper face of GG, and hence dimF⁡(K,z)≤n−k−1\dim F(K,z)\leq n-k-1. Property (Ik−1,n−k−1)(I_{k-1,n-k-1}) then implies that T∨F⁡(K,z)T\vee F(K,z) is proper. Since y,z∈T∨F⁡(K,z)y,z\in T\vee F(K,z), we have g∈relint⁡G∩(T∨F⁡(K,z))g\in\operatorname{relint}G\cap\big(T\vee F(K,z)\big), and Lemma 2.2 gives G⊆T∨F⁡(K,z)G\subseteq T\vee F(K,z). As F⊆T∨F⁡(K,z)F\subseteq T\vee F(K,z) as well, F∨GF\vee G is a face of T∨F⁡(K,z)T\vee F(K,z), which is proper. Therefore F∨GF\vee G is a proper face of KK. ∎

We are therefore left with the case where dim(F∨G′)≥k\dim(F\vee G^{\prime})\geq k.

Lemma 5.3.

Let K∈𝒦nK\in\mathcal{K}^{n} be a full-dimensional convex body. Let FF and GG be proper faces of KK satisfying the following properties:

(26) if ​F′​ is a proper face of ​F, then ​F′∨G​ is a proper face of ​K;\displaystyle\text{if }F^{\prime}\text{ is a proper face of }F,\text{ then }F^{\prime}\vee G\text{ is a proper face of }K;
(27) if ​G′​ is a proper face of ​G, then ​F∨G′​ is a proper face of ​K.\displaystyle\text{if }G^{\prime}\text{ is a proper face of }G,\text{ then }F\vee G^{\prime}\text{ is a proper face of }K.

Then one of the following holds:

  1. (a)

    F∨GF\vee G is proper;

  2. (b)

    FF and GG are affinely independent, K∩aff⁡(F,G)=conv⁡(F,G)K\cap\operatorname{aff}(F,G)=\operatorname{conv}(F,G), and for any extreme point y∈Gy\in G one has

    (28) (F∨y)∩aff⁡(F,G)=conv⁡(F,y).\displaystyle(F\vee y)\cap\operatorname{aff}(F,G)=\operatorname{conv}(F,y).
Proof.

We fix u∈relint⁡Fu\in\operatorname{relint}F and v∈relint⁡Gv\in\operatorname{relint}G for the rest of the proof and put o:=(u+v)/2o:=(u+v)/2. Then we have o∈relint⁡conv⁡(F,G)o\in\operatorname{relint}\operatorname{conv}(F,G). If o∈∂Ko\in\partial K, we can find a proper face HH of KK containing oo. Then u,v∈Hu,v\in H, and Lemma 2.2 implies that HH must also contain FF and GG. Therefore F∨G⊆HF\vee G\subseteq H is a proper face of KK, and item (a) holds in this case. In the following we will assume o∈int⁡Ko\in\operatorname{int}K and aim to prove the second claim. We will denote S:=aff⁡(F,G)S:=\operatorname{aff}(F,G) and Q:=conv⁡(F,G)Q:=\operatorname{conv}(F,G).

To prove that FF and GG are affinely independent, we must show dimS=dimF+dimG+1\dim S=\dim F+\dim G+1. To this end, we consider the convex body

Q^:={((1−t)f,tg,t):f∈F,g∈G, 0≤t≤1}∈𝒦2​n+1,\widehat{Q}:=\left\{((1-t)f,tg,t):f\in F,\ g\in G,\ 0\leq t\leq 1\right\}\in\mathcal{K}^{2n+1},

i.e., the convex hull of F×{0}×{0}F\times\{0\}\times\{0\} and {0}×G×{1}\{0\}\times G\times\{1\}, and the linear map π:ℝn×ℝn×ℝ→ℝn\pi:\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^{n} given by π⁡(a,b,t):=a+b\pi(a,b,t):=a+b. Observe that π⁡(Q^)=Q\pi(\widehat{Q})=Q, hence π⁡(aff⁡Q^)=S\pi(\operatorname{aff}\widehat{Q})=S. Because dimaff⁡Q^=dimF+dimG+1\dim\operatorname{aff}\widehat{Q}=\dim F+\dim G+1, it suffices to show that π|aff⁡Q^\pi|_{\operatorname{aff}\widehat{Q}} is injective.

We will first show that π⁡(relbd⁡Q^)⊆∂K\pi(\operatorname{relbd}\widehat{Q})\subseteq\partial K. We have

relbd⁡Q^=R1∪R2∪(⋃f∈relbd⁡FR3,f)∪(⋃g∈relbd⁡GR4,g),\operatorname{relbd}\widehat{Q}=R_{1}\cup R_{2}\cup\left(\bigcup_{f\in\operatorname{relbd}F}R_{3,f}\right)\cup\left(\bigcup_{g\in\operatorname{relbd}G}R_{4,g}\right),

where

R1\displaystyle R_{1} :=F×{0}×{0},\displaystyle:=F\times\{0\}\times\{0\},
R2\displaystyle R_{2} :={0}×G×{1},\displaystyle:=\{0\}\times G\times\{1\},
R3,f\displaystyle R_{3,f} :={((1−t)f,tg,t):0<t<1,g∈G},f∈relbdF,\displaystyle:=\left\{\big((1-t)f,tg,t\big):0<t<1,\,g\in G\right\},\quad f\in\operatorname{relbd}F,
R4,g\displaystyle R_{4,g} :={((1−t)f,tg,t):0<t<1,f∈F},g∈relbdG.\displaystyle:=\left\{\big((1-t)f,tg,t\big):0<t<1,\,f\in F\right\},\quad g\in\operatorname{relbd}G.

Since FF and GG are proper faces of KK, π⁡(R1)\pi(R_{1}) and π⁡(R2)\pi(R_{2}) are contained in ∂K\partial K. Since every f∈relbd⁡Ff\in\operatorname{relbd}F lies in a proper face F′F^{\prime} of FF, (26) implies π⁡(R3,f)⊆F′∨G⊆∂K\pi(R_{3,f})\subseteq F^{\prime}\vee G\subseteq\partial K. Similarly, using (27), we get π⁡(R4,g)⊆∂K\pi(R_{4,g})\subseteq\partial K for every g∈relbd⁡Gg\in\operatorname{relbd}G. We thus conclude π⁡(relbd⁡Q^)⊆∂K\pi(\operatorname{relbd}\widehat{Q})\subseteq\partial K.

Consider the point o^:=(u/2,v/2,1/2)∈relint⁡Q^\widehat{o}:=(u/2,v/2,1/2)\in\operatorname{relint}\widehat{Q}. It satisfies π⁡(o^)=o\pi(\widehat{o})=o. Fix an arbitrary nonzero w∈ℝn×ℝn×ℝw\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\mathbb{R} such that o^+w∈aff⁡Q^\widehat{o}+w\in\operatorname{aff}\widehat{Q}. Then the ray {o^+tw\{\widehat{o}+tw: t∈(0,+∞)}t\in(0,+\infty)\} intersects the relative boundary of Q^\widehat{Q}. That is, there is r>0r>0 such that o^+r​w∈relbd⁡Q^\widehat{o}+rw\in\operatorname{relbd}\widehat{Q}. For the claim K∩S=QK\cap S=Q, note first that K∩S⊇QK\cap S\supseteq Q holds because S=aff⁡QS=\operatorname{aff}Q. For the reverse inclusion, assume for contradiction that there exists x∈(K∩S)∖Qx\in(K\cap S)\setminus Q. In particular, x∈aff⁡Q∖Qx\in\operatorname{aff}Q\setminus Q. Since o∈relint⁡Qo\in\operatorname{relint}Q, the open segment (o,x)(o,x) intersects relbd⁡Q⊆∂K\operatorname{relbd}Q\subseteq\partial K at some point yy. Finally, choose an extreme point y∈Gy\in G and set D:=F∨yD:=F\vee y. To prove (28), observe first that both sides are faces of conv⁡(F,G)\operatorname{conv}(F,G). On the other hand, DD is a face of KK, so D∩SD\cap S is a face of K∩S=conv⁡(F,G)K\cap S=\operatorname{conv}(F,G). Next, put p:=(u+y)/2p:=(u+y)/2. Since y∉aff⁡Fy\notin\operatorname{aff}F, we have p∈relint⁡conv⁡(F,y)p\in\operatorname{relint}\operatorname{conv}(F,y). By Lemma 2.3, pp also lies in relint⁡D\operatorname{relint}D and hence in relint⁡(D∩S)\operatorname{relint}(D\cap S). Consequently, relint⁡(D∩S)∩relint⁡conv⁡(F,y)≠∅\operatorname{relint}(D\cap S)\cap\operatorname{relint}\operatorname{conv}(F,y)\neq\emptyset. Now Lemma 2.2 applied twice implies D∩S=conv⁡(F,y)D\cap S=\operatorname{conv}(F,y), as claimed. ∎

Lemma 5.4.

Let 2≤k≤n−12\leq k\leq n-1, and suppose that K∈𝒦nK\in\mathcal{K}^{n} satisfies (Ik−1,n−k−1)(I_{k-1,n-k-1}). Let FF and GG be faces of KK with dimF=k\dim F=k and dimG=n−k\dim G=n-k, such that F∩G={y}F\cap G=\{y\} for some y∈Ky\in K and aff⁡(F,G)=ℝn\operatorname{aff}(F,G)=\mathbb{R}^{n}. Then conv⁡(F,G)=K\operatorname{conv}(F,G)=K.

Proof.

Translate KK so that y=0y=0. Then U:=aff⁡FU:=\operatorname{aff}F and V:=aff⁡GV:=\operatorname{aff}G are complementary linear subspaces, that is, ℝn=U⊕V\mathbb{R}^{n}=U\oplus V. In particular, dimconv⁡(F,G)=n\dim\operatorname{conv}(F,G)=n. Since conv⁡(F,G)⊆K\operatorname{conv}(F,G)\subseteq K it suffices to show ∂(conv⁡(F,G))⊆∂K\partial(\operatorname{conv}(F,G))\subseteq\partial K.

Observe that we in fact have 0∈relbd⁡F∩relbd⁡G0\in\operatorname{relbd}F\cap\operatorname{relbd}G. Indeed, if for instance 0∈relint⁡F0\in\operatorname{relint}F, Lemma 2.2 implies that F⊆GF\subseteq G, and hence UU and VV cannot be linearly independent.

We claim that every point z∈∂(conv⁡(F,G))z\in\partial(\operatorname{conv}(F,G)) lies in a segment [f,g][f,g] with f∈relbd⁡Ff\in\operatorname{relbd}F and g∈relbd⁡Gg\in\operatorname{relbd}G. The case z=0z=0 is immediate, since 0∈relbd⁡F∩relbd⁡G0\in\operatorname{relbd}F\cap\operatorname{relbd}G. If z∈F∖{0}z\in F\setminus\{0\}, the ray from 00 through zz intersects relbd⁡F\operatorname{relbd}F at ff. Then z∈[0,f]z\in[0,f] as required. The case z∈G∖{0}z\in G\setminus\{0\} follows similarly. Otherwise, write z=t​f0+(1−t)​g0z=tf_{0}+(1-t)g_{0} with 0<t<10<t<1, f0∈Ff_{0}\in F, and g0∈Gg_{0}\in G. If f0∈relbd⁡Ff_{0}\in\operatorname{relbd}F and g0∈relbd⁡Gg_{0}\in\operatorname{relbd}G, we are already done. Hence we assume for example f0∈relint⁡Ff_{0}\in\operatorname{relint}F. By Lemma 2.2, F⊆HF\subseteq H. So 0∈H0\in H and H∩GH\cap G is a proper face of GG. Then g∈[0,g0]⊆H∩G⊆relbd⁡Gg\in[0,g_{0}]\subseteq H\cap G\subseteq\operatorname{relbd}G and z=t​ρ​f+(1−t​ρ)​gz=t\rho f+(1-t\rho)g. This shows the existence of f∈relbd⁡F,g∈relbd⁡Gf\in\operatorname{relbd}F,\,g\in\operatorname{relbd}G with z∈[f,g]z\in[f,g] in this case. The case g0∈relint⁡Gg_{0}\in\operatorname{relint}G is analogous.

Fix z∈∂(conv⁡(F,G))z\in\partial(\operatorname{conv}(F,G)) and choose f,gf,g as above. Since f∈relbd⁡Ff\in\operatorname{relbd}F, we have dimF⁡(K,f)≤dimF−1=k−1\dim F(K,f)\leq\dim F-1=k-1. Similarly, dimF⁡(K,g)≤n−k−1\dim F(K,g)\leq n-k-1. Property (Ik−1,n−k−1)(I_{k-1,n-k-1}) therefore implies that f,gf,g are contained in a proper face of KK. In particular, z∈[f,g]⊆F⁡(K,{f,g})⊆∂Kz\in[f,g]\subseteq F(K,\{f,g\})\subseteq\partial K. Since zz was chosen arbitrarily, we conclude ∂(conv⁡(F,G))⊆∂K\partial(\operatorname{conv}(F,G))\subseteq\partial K.

∎

Lemma 5.5.

Let 1≤k≤n−11\leq k\leq n-1, and let D,G∈𝒦nD,G\in\mathcal{K}^{n} with dimD=k\dim D=k and dimG=n−k\dim G=n-k, such that 0∈D∩G0\in D\cap G and D∪GD\cup G spans ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. Let FF be a face of DD with 0∉F0\notin F. Then there is a face TT of conv⁡(D,G)\operatorname{conv}(D,G) containing FF, meeting GG, and satisfying dimT=dimF+1\dim T=\dim F+1.

Proof.

Put C:=conv⁡(D,G)C:=\operatorname{conv}(D,G), U:=aff⁡DU:=\operatorname{aff}D, and V:=aff⁡GV:=\operatorname{aff}G. Since 0∈D∩G0\in D\cap G, the hypotheses give ℝn=U⊕V\mathbb{R}^{n}=U\oplus V. Choose a nonzero extreme point ww of GG, and set T:=conv⁡(F,w)T:=\operatorname{conv}(F,w). Our choice of ww implies w∈T∩Gw\in T\cap G and w∉Uw\notin U, so dimT=dimF+1\dim T=\dim F+1.

To verify the face property, suppose z∈Tz\in T and z=λ​x1+(1−λ)​x2z=\lambda x_{1}+(1-\lambda)x_{2}, where x1,x2∈Cx_{1},x_{2}\in C, 0<λ<10<\lambda<1. We need to show that x1,x2∈Tx_{1},x_{2}\in T.

Write xi=αi​di+(1−αi)​gix_{i}=\alpha_{i}d_{i}+(1-\alpha_{i})g_{i}, where di∈Dd_{i}\in D, gi∈Gg_{i}\in G, and 0≤αi≤10\leq\alpha_{i}\leq 1, for i=1,2i=1,2. Put r:=λ​α1+(1−λ)​α2r:=\lambda\alpha_{1}+(1-\lambda)\alpha_{2}. Since z∈Tz\in T, we also have z=t​f+(1−t)​wz=tf+(1-t)w, for some f∈Ff\in F and 0≤t≤10\leq t\leq 1. Together, we have

t​f+(1−t)​w=z=λ⁡(α1​d1+(1−α1)​g1)+(1−λ)​(α2​d2+(1−α2)​g2).tf+(1-t)w=z=\lambda(\alpha_{1}d_{1}+(1-\alpha_{1})g_{1})+(1-\lambda)(\alpha_{2}d_{2}+(1-\alpha_{2})g_{2}).

Taking the components in UU and VV respectively gives

(29) t​f\displaystyle tf =λ​α1​d1+(1−λ)​α2​d2,\displaystyle=\lambda\alpha_{1}d_{1}+(1-\lambda)\alpha_{2}d_{2},
(30) (1−t)​w\displaystyle(1-t)w =λ⁡(1−α1)​g1+(1−λ)​(1−α2)​g2.\displaystyle=\lambda(1-\alpha_{1})g_{1}+(1-\lambda)(1-\alpha_{2})g_{2}.

We claim that this implies r=tr=t. Indeed, if r<tr<t, then (29) implies

f=λ​α1t​d1+(1−λ)​α2t​d2+(1−rt)​0.f=\frac{\lambda\alpha_{1}}{t}d_{1}+\frac{(1-\lambda)\alpha_{2}}{t}d_{2}+\left(1-\frac{r}{t}\right)0.

Hence ff is a convex combination of points where 00 has a positive coefficient. Since f∈Ff\in F, we have 0∈F0\in F, a contradiction. If r>tr>t, then (30) implies

w=λ⁡(1−α1)1−t​g1+(1−λ)​(1−α2)1−t​g2+r−t1−t​0.w=\frac{\lambda(1-\alpha_{1})}{1-t}g_{1}+\frac{(1-\lambda)(1-\alpha_{2})}{1-t}g_{2}+\frac{r-t}{1-t}0.

However, ww is an extreme point, hence cannot be written as a nontrivial convex combination of points in GG, a contradiction. We thus have r=tr=t and will distinguish three cases.

First, if t=0t=0, then r=0r=0 forces α1=α2=0\alpha_{1}=\alpha_{2}=0. Thus x1,x2∈Gx_{1},x_{2}\in G, and (30) together with extremality of ww in GG gives x1=x2=w∈Tx_{1}=x_{2}=w\in T.

Second, if t=1t=1, then r=1r=1 forces α1=α2=1\alpha_{1}=\alpha_{2}=1. Thus x1,x2∈Dx_{1},x_{2}\in D, and (29) together with the face property of FF in DD gives x1,x2∈F⊆Tx_{1},x_{2}\in F\subseteq T.

Finally, assume 0<t<10<t<1. Then by (29) and (30) we have the convex combinations

(31) f\displaystyle f =λ​α1t​d1+(1−λ)​α2t​d2,\displaystyle=\frac{\lambda\alpha_{1}}{t}d_{1}+\frac{(1-\lambda)\alpha_{2}}{t}d_{2},
(32) w\displaystyle w =λ⁡(1−α1)1−t​g1+(1−λ)​(1−α2)1−t​g2.\displaystyle=\frac{\lambda(1-\alpha_{1})}{1-t}g_{1}+\frac{(1-\lambda)(1-\alpha_{2})}{1-t}g_{2}.

If αi>0\alpha_{i}>0, then (31) together with the face property of FF in DD implies di∈Fd_{i}\in F. If αi<1\alpha_{i}<1, then (32) together with extremality of ww in GG implies gi=wg_{i}=w. An easy case distinction then shows that xi=αi​di+(1−αi)​gi∈conv⁡(F,w)x_{i}=\alpha_{i}d_{i}+(1-\alpha_{i})g_{i}\in\operatorname{conv}(F,w), i=1,2i=1,2, for any (α1,α2)∈[0,1]2(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2})\in[0,1]^{2}. ∎

Lemma 5.6.

Let 2≤k≤n−12\leq k\leq n-1 and 0≤d≤k−20\leq d\leq k-2. Let K∈𝒦nK\in\mathcal{K}^{n} be a full-dimensional convex body satisfying (Ik−1,n−k−1)(I_{k-1,n-k-1}). Assume that FF and GG are faces of KK satisfying dimF=d\dim F=d, dimG=n−k\dim G=n-k, and (26). Then F∨GF\vee G is proper.

Proof.

Let G′G^{\prime} be a proper face of GG. Then dimG′≤n−k−1\dim G^{\prime}\leq n-k-1 and (Ik−1,n−k−1)(I_{k-1,n-k-1}) implies that F∨G′F\vee G^{\prime} is proper. Hence, FF and GG also satisfy (27) and we may use Lemma 5.3. If item (a) in Lemma 5.3 holds, then we are done. Therefore, we assume from now on that item (b) holds. Choose an extreme point yy of GG and denote D:=F∨yD:=F\vee y. We will also denote S:=aff⁡(F,G)S:=\operatorname{aff}(F,G). Then FF and GG are affinely independent, K∩S=conv⁡(F,G)K\cap S=\operatorname{conv}(F,G), and D∩S=conv⁡(F,y)D\cap S=\operatorname{conv}(F,y).

Property (Ik−1,n−k−1)(I_{k-1,n-k-1}) implies that DD is proper. Moreover, since FF and GG are affinely independent, we have

dimS\displaystyle\dim S =dimF+dimG+1=d+n−k+1,\displaystyle=\dim F+\dim G+1=d+n-k+1,
dimconv⁡(F,y)\displaystyle\dim\operatorname{conv}(F,y) =dimF+1=d+1,\displaystyle=\dim F+1=d+1,

and therefore

(33) dimD≤dim(D∩S)+codim⁡(S)=dimconv⁡(F,y)+n−dimS=k.\dim D\leq\dim(D\cap S)+\operatorname{codim}(S)=\dim\operatorname{conv}(F,y)+n-\dim S=k.

If dimD≤k−1\dim D\leq k-1, then taking T=DT=D in Lemma 5.2 shows that F∨GF\vee G is proper as desired.

It remains to treat the case dimD=k\dim D=k. In this case, (33) takes equality, which yields aff⁡(D,S)=ℝn\operatorname{aff}(D,S)=\mathbb{R}^{n}. Since F⊆DF\subseteq D and S=aff⁡(F,G)S=\operatorname{aff}(F,G), we have aff⁡(D,G)=ℝn\operatorname{aff}(D,G)=\mathbb{R}^{n}. Moreover, D∩G=conv⁡(F,y)∩G={y}D\cap G=\operatorname{conv}(F,y)\cap G=\{y\}. We may therefore apply Lemma 5.4 to D,GD,G, which gives K=conv⁡(D,G)K=\operatorname{conv}(D,G). Since FF is a proper face of DD and translating KK so that y=0y=0, Lemma 5.5 implies that there is a face TT of KK containing FF, intersecting GG, and satisfying dimT=d+1≤k−1\dim T=d+1\leq k-1. Applying Lemma 5.2 to this TT shows that F∨GF\vee G is proper. ∎

Next we will show by induction that the assumption (26) on the faces FF and GG in the previous lemma can in fact be omitted.

Lemma 5.7.

Let 2≤k≤n−12\leq k\leq n-1 and 0≤d≤k−20\leq d\leq k-2. Let K∈𝒦nK\in\mathcal{K}^{n} be a full-dimensional convex body satisfying (Ik−1,n−k−1)(I_{k-1,n-k-1}). Assume that FF and GG are faces of KK satisfying dimF=d\dim F=d and dimG=n−k\dim G=n-k. Then F∨GF\vee G is proper.

Proof.

We argue by strong induction on dd. First, if d=0d=0, then there is no proper face of FF. Hence (26) holds trivially and the claim follows immediately from Lemma 5.6. Second, fix d>0d>0 and assume the statement holds for 0,…,d−10,\dots,d-1. For every proper face F′F^{\prime} of FF, we have dimF′<d\dim F^{\prime}<d and hence the induction hypothesis implies that F′∨GF^{\prime}\vee G is proper. Thus (26) holds and the claim follows again from Lemma 5.6. ∎

Now we can finally proceed to the proof of the induction step in Theorem 1.4.

Proposition 5.8.

Let K∈𝒦nK\in\mathcal{K}^{n} be a full-dimensional convex body and 2≤k≤n−12\leq k\leq n-1. If KK satisfies (Ik−1,n−k−1)(I_{k-1,n-k-1}), then it satisfies (Ik−2,n−k)(I_{k-2,n-k}).

Proof.

Take any faces F,GF,G of KK with dimF≤k−2\dim F\leq k-2 and dimG≤n−k\dim G\leq n-k. If dimG≤n−k−1\dim G\leq n-k-1, property (Ik−1,n−k−1)(I_{k-1,n-k-1}) gives that F∨GF\vee G is proper. Otherwise, dimG=n−k\dim G=n-k, and the same conclusion follows from Lemma 5.7, applied with d=dimFd=\dim F. Since FF and GG were arbitrary, KK satisfies (Ik−2,n−k)(I_{k-2,n-k}). ∎

5.2. The k=1k=1 case

It remains to prove the base case. Recall that we assume n≥2n\geq 2.

Lemma 5.9.

Let K∈𝒦nK\in\mathcal{K}^{n} be a full-dimensional convex body. If KK satisfies (I0,n−2)(I_{0,n-2}), then KK is a simplex.

Proof.

Let xx be an arbitrary extreme point of KK and put F:={x}F:=\{x\}. Choose p∈int⁡Kp\in\interior K and let b∈∂Kb\in\partial K be the (unique) point such that p∈[b,x]p\in[b,x]. Denote G:=F⁡(K,b)G:=F(K,b). Then F∨GF\vee G contains p∈int⁡Kp\in\interior K and thus F∨G=KF\vee G=K. Since KK satisfies (I0,n−2)(I_{0,n-2}), we have dimG=n−1\dim G=n-1. Moreover, for any proper face G′G^{\prime} of GG, one has dimG′≤n−2\dim G^{\prime}\leq n-2 and hence by (I0,n−2)(I_{0,n-2}), F∨G′F\vee G^{\prime} is proper. This shows that (27) holds. Note also that (26) holds trivially since FF has no proper faces. We may therefore apply Lemma 5.3. Since F∨G=KF\vee G=K, item (a) of Lemma 5.3 cannot hold. Hence FF and GG are affinely independent and one has

K=K∩aff⁡(F,G)=conv⁡(F,G)=conv⁡(G,x).K=K\cap\operatorname{aff}(F,G)=\operatorname{conv}(F,G)=\operatorname{conv}(G,x).

We thus conclude that KK is a pyramid with base GG and apex xx. In particular, every extreme point of KK other than xx belongs to GG and so xx does not lie in the affine hull of the other extreme points.

Since xx was arbitrary, we get that every finite set of extreme points of KK is affinely independent and consequently KK has at most n+1n+1 extreme points. Since KK is full-dimensional and equal to the convex hull of its extreme points, we conclude that KK is an nn-simplex. ∎

5.3. Proof of Theorems 1.4 and 1.2

Proof of Theorem 1.4.

First, assume that KK satisfies (b) or, in other words, the property (Ik−1,n−k−1)(I_{k-1,n-k-1}). Applying Proposition 5.8 repeatedly, this implies that KK satisfies (I0,n−2)(I_{0,n-2}). Now Lemma 5.9 shows that KK is a simplex.

Conversely, assume that KK is a simplex and F,GF,G are faces of KK with dimF≤k−1\dim F\leq k-1 and dimG≤n−k−1\dim G\leq n-k-1. Since FF and GG are simplices themselves, they together contain at most k+(n−k)=nk+(n-k)=n vertices of KK. Hence there is a vertex y∈Ky\in K not contained in F∪GF\cup G. Choose HH to be the facet of KK not containing yy. Then F∨G⊆HF\vee G\subseteq H and (b) follows.

Next, translate KK so that it contains the origin in its interior and assume that K∘K^{\circ} satisfies (b). Consider u,v∈𝕊n−1u,v\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1} such that dimT⁡(K,u)≤k\dim T(K,u)\leq k and dimT⁡(K,v)≤n−k\dim T(K,v)\leq n-k. By Lemma 2.4, F:=T⁡(K,u)∩∂K∘F:=T(K,u)\cap\partial K^{\circ} and G:=T⁡(K,v)∩∂K∘G:=T(K,v)\cap\partial K^{\circ} are faces of K∘K^{\circ} satisfying dimF≤k−1\dim F\leq k-1 and dimG≤n−k−1\dim G\leq n-k-1. Therefore, the face F∨GF\vee G is proper. Using Lemma 2.4, we have ℝ≥0​(F∨G)=T⁡(K,w)\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}(F\vee G)=T(K,w) for some w∈𝕊n−1w\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1}. The touching cone T⁡(K,w)T(K,w) clearly contains both T⁡(K,u)T(K,u) and T⁡(K,v)T(K,v), and we conclude that KK satisfies (c).

Conversely, assume that KK satisfies (c), and let F,GF,G be proper faces of K∘K^{\circ} such that dimF≤k−1\dim F\leq k-1 and dimG≤n−k−1\dim G\leq n-k-1. By Lemma 2.4, there exist u,v∈𝕊n−1u,v\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1} with ℝ≥0​F=T⁡(K,u)\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}F=T(K,u) and ℝ≥0​G=T⁡(K,v)\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}G=T(K,v). Then dimT⁡(K,u)≤k\dim T(K,u)\leq k and dimT⁡(K,v)≤n−k\dim T(K,v)\leq n-k, and hence condition (c) in turn ensures that there exists some w∈𝕊n−1w\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1} such that T⁡(K,w)T(K,w) contains both T⁡(K,u)T(K,u) and T⁡(K,v)T(K,v). By Lemma 2.4, T⁡(K,w)∩∂K∘T(K,w)\cap\partial K^{\circ} is a proper face of K∘K^{\circ}. Since it clearly contains both FF and GG, F∨GF\vee G is proper. We conclude that K∘K^{\circ} satisfies (b).

Finally, observing that K∈𝒦onK\in\mathcal{K}^{n}_{o} is a simplex if and only if K∘K^{\circ} is a simplex and using the previously shown equivalence (a)⇔\iff(b), we have that KK satisfies (c) if and only if KK is a simplex. This finishes the proof. ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.2.

This follows immediately by combining Proposition 1.3 with Theorem 1.4. ∎

6. Equality cases of the higher-order Godbersen inequality

In this last section we prove Theorem 1.8 by reducing the incidence condition for p+1p+1 faces to the two-face condition of Theorem 1.4. Combined with Proposition 1.7, this completes the proof of equality characterization in Theorem 1.5.

The following proposition, which we will require for the reduction, is most probably known. However, since we have no suitable reference, we provide a proof here for completeness.

Proposition 6.1.

Let K∈𝒦nK\in\mathcal{K}^{n} be a full-dimensional convex body. Let f,g≥1f,g\geq 1 be integers such that f+g≥n+1f+g\geq n+1. Then there exist proper faces F,GF,G of KK such that

dimF≤f−1,dimG≤g−1,andF∨G=K.\dim F\leq f-1,\qquad\dim G\leq g-1,\qquad\text{and}\qquad F\vee G=K.
Proof.

Without loss of generality we may assume f+g=n+1f+g=n+1. We will inductively construct two sequences (Fj)(F_{j}) and (Gj)(G_{j}), j=0,1,…j=0,1,\dots, of proper faces of KK satisfying Fj∨Gj=KF_{j}\vee G_{j}=K, dimFj≤f−1\dim F_{j}\leq f-1 and (26), (27) from Lemma 5.3.

First, we may always write K=x1∨⋯∨xmK=x_{1}\vee\dots\vee x_{m} where mm is an integer and x1,…,xmx_{1},\dots,x_{m} are extreme points of KK. Let us fix such a representation of KK with minimal mm. We let F0:={x1}F_{0}:=\{x_{1}\} and G0G_{0} be a minimal face of x2∨⋯∨xmx_{2}\vee\dots\vee x_{m} such that F0∨G0=KF_{0}\vee G_{0}=K. It is clear that F0,G0F_{0},G_{0} are faces of KK with the required properties.

Second, assume that Fj,Gj⊆KF_{j},G_{j}\subseteq K are as above. If dimGj≤g−1\dim G_{j}\leq g-1, we set Fj+1:=FjF_{j+1}:=F_{j} and Gj+1:=GjG_{j+1}:=G_{j}. If dimGj≥g\dim G_{j}\geq g, we proceed as follows: Pick a maximal proper face G~⊆Gj\widetilde{G}\subseteq G_{j}. Then there exists an extreme point y∈Gjy\in G_{j} not contained in G~\widetilde{G}. We set F~:=Fj∨y\widetilde{F}:=F_{j}\vee y. By Lemma 5.3, FjF_{j} and GjG_{j} are affinely independent and satisfy (28). The former implies

dimaff⁡(Fj,Gj)=dimFj+dimGj+1,\dim\operatorname{aff}(F_{j},G_{j})=\dim F_{j}+\dim G_{j}+1,

the latter yields aff⁡(F~∩aff⁡(Fj,Gj))=aff⁡(Fj,y)\operatorname{aff}(\widetilde{F}\cap\operatorname{aff}(F_{j},G_{j}))=\operatorname{aff}(F_{j},y). Consequently,

dimF~\displaystyle\dim\widetilde{F} ≤dimaff⁡(F~∩aff⁡(Fj,Gj))+codim⁡aff⁡(Fj,Gj)\displaystyle\leq\dim\operatorname{aff}(\widetilde{F}\cap\operatorname{aff}(F_{j},G_{j}))+\operatorname{codim}\operatorname{aff}(F_{j},G_{j})
=dimFj+1+n−(dimFj+dimGj+1)\displaystyle=\dim F_{j}+1+n-(\dim F_{j}+\dim G_{j}+1)
=n−dimGj\displaystyle=n-\dim G_{j}
≤f−1,\displaystyle\leq f-1,

where in the last step we used our assumptions f+g=n+1f+g=n+1 and dimGj≥g\dim G_{j}\geq g. Using the maximality of G~\widetilde{G}, we further have

F~∨G~=Fj∨y∨G~=Fj∨Gj=K.\widetilde{F}\vee\widetilde{G}=F_{j}\vee y\vee\widetilde{G}=F_{j}\vee G_{j}=K.

We choose faces Fj+1⊆F~F_{j+1}\subseteq\widetilde{F} and Gj+1⊆G~G_{j+1}\subseteq\widetilde{G} satisfying Fj+1∨Gj+1=KF_{j+1}\vee G_{j+1}=K and minimizing dimFj+1+dimGj+1\dim F_{j+1}+\dim G_{j+1}. Then we have dimFj+1≤dimF~≤f−1\dim F_{j+1}\leq\dim\widetilde{F}\leq f-1, and the minimality of dimFj+1+dimGj+1\dim F_{j+1}+\dim G_{j+1} implies that Fj+1,Gj+1F_{j+1},G_{j+1} satisfy (26) and (27). Note that Fj+1,Gj+1F_{j+1},G_{j+1} are clearly proper faces of KK since Fj,GjF_{j},G_{j} were such.

Observe that, if dimGj≥g\dim G_{j}\geq g, we have dimGj+1<dimGj\dim G_{j+1}<\dim G_{j} since G~⊆Gj\widetilde{G}\subseteq G_{j} was proper. Therefore, there exists j0≥0j_{0}\geq 0 such that dimGj0≤g−1\dim G_{j_{0}}\leq g-1 and we thus may take F:=Fj0F:=F_{j_{0}} and G:=Gj0G:=G_{j_{0}} to finish the proof. ∎

It will be convenient to generalize Definition 5.1 to the higher-order setting.

Definition 6.2.

Let K∈𝒦nK\in\mathcal{K}^{n} and fix integers p≥1p\geq 1 and q0,…,qp≥0q_{0},\dots,q_{p}\geq 0. We say that KK satisfies property (Iq0,…,qp)(I_{q_{0},\dots,q_{p}}) if for any faces F0,…,FpF_{0},\dots,F_{p} of KK with dimFi≤qi\dim F_{i}\leq q_{i}, i=0,…,pi=0,\dots,p, the face F0∨⋯∨FpF_{0}\vee\cdots\vee F_{p} is proper.

Lemma 6.3.

Let K∈𝒦nK\in\mathcal{K}^{n}, p≥2p\geq 2, and q0,…,qp≥0q_{0},\dots,q_{p}\geq 0. If KK satisfies (Iq0,…,qp)(I_{q_{0},\dots,q_{p}}), then it satisfies (Iq0,…,qp−2,qp−1+qp+1)(I_{q_{0},\dots,q_{p-2},q_{p-1}+q_{p}+1}).

Proof.

Assume that KK satisfies (Iq0,…,qp)(I_{q_{0},\dots,q_{p}}) and consider any faces F0,…,Fp−1⊆KF_{0},\dots,F_{p-1}\subseteq K with

dimFi≤qi,i=0,…,p−2,anddimFp−1≤qp−1+qp+1.\dim F_{i}\leq q_{i},\quad i=0,\dots,p-2,\qquad\text{and}\qquad\dim F_{p-1}\leq q_{p-1}+q_{p}+1.

By Proposition 6.1, there exist faces F,G⊆Fp−1F,G\subseteq F_{p-1} such that dimF≤qp−1\dim F\leq q_{p-1}, dimG≤qp\dim G\leq q_{p}, and F∨G=Fp−1F\vee G=F_{p-1}. By (Iq0,…,qp)(I_{q_{0},\dots,q_{p}}), F0∨⋯∨Fp−1=F0∨⋯∨Fp−2∨F∨GF_{0}\vee\cdots\vee F_{p-1}=F_{0}\vee\cdots\vee F_{p-2}\vee F\vee G is a proper face of KK, and hence KK satisfies (Iq0,…,qp−2,qp−1+qp+1)(I_{q_{0},\dots,q_{p-2},q_{p-1}+q_{p}+1}). ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.8.

First, assume that KK satisfies (b) or, in other words, the property (Ik0−1,…,kp−1)(I_{k_{0}-1,\dots,k_{p}-1}). Applying Lemma 6.3 repeatedly and using ∑i=0pki=n\sum_{i=0}^{p}k_{i}=n, this implies that KK satisfies (Ik0−1,n−k0−1)(I_{k_{0}-1,n-k_{0}-1}). Now Theorem 1.4 implies that KK is a simplex.

Conversely, assume that KK is a simplex and F0,…,FpF_{0},\dots,F_{p} are faces of KK with dimFi≤ki−1\dim F_{i}\leq k_{i}-1, i=0,…,pi=0,\dots,p. Since F0,…,FpF_{0},\dots,F_{p} are simplices themselves, they together contain at most ∑i=0pki=n\sum_{i=0}^{p}k_{i}=n vertices of KK. Hence there is a vertex y∈Ky\in K not contained in any FiF_{i}, i=0,…,pi=0,\dots,p. Choosing F⊆KF\subseteq K to be the facet not containing yy, (b) follows.

Finally, translate KK so that it contains the origin in its interior. Then a straightforward generalization of the corresponding part of the proof of Theorem 1.4, that is, an easy application of Lemma 2.4, shows that KK satisfies (c) if and only if K∘K^{\circ} satisfies (b). By the previously shown equivalence (a)⇔\iff(b), we thus have that KK satisfies (c) if and only if K∘K^{\circ} is a simplex. Using the self-duality property of a simplex, we conclude that (a)⇔\iff(c). This finishes the proof. ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.5.

The inequality (7) was proven in Proposition 3.1. By Remark 1.6, it remains to characterize the equality cases when KK is full-dimensional and k0,…,kp≥1k_{0},\dots,k_{p}\geq 1 (and hence p≤n−1p\leq n-1). In this case, it follows immediately from Proposition 1.7 and Theorem 1.8 that KK attains equality in (7) if and only if KK is a simplex. ∎
